speechtext:
I wish to rise to a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. It arises out of an interjection made last night by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) when I was speaking in the debate. The minister questioned the accuracy of some of the figures I had quoted. If hon. members will refer to page 110 of Hansard they will find these remarks reported:
Mr. Howe:	What are you talking about?
What about the years 1943, 1944 and 1945?
Mr. Bracken:	If the minister wishes to base
an argument upon what happened during the war years when the United States was buying war equipment, he can do so.
Mr. Howe:	I am speaking to a matter of
privilege. I do not wish to base an argument; but I wish my hon. friend to tell the truth about it.
Then at another place on page 105:
Mr. Howe:	My hon. friend has overlooked
the minus signs. We had a strong balance of trade with the United States in 1943, 1944 and 1945.
I just wish to say, Mr. Speaker, that; the figures I was using were taken from a document published by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics of the Department of Trade and Commerce. We took the records of the exports and imports, separated them, and showed the balance. Since the question has been raised as to the accuracy of the figures I used, and the minister having raised this point about the years 1943, 1944 and 1945, I think the matter should be set straight. The imports from the United States for those three years according to this publication were:
Millions
1943		 $1,423,672,486
1944		 1,447,225.915
1945		 1,202,417,634
The exports to the United States in those years were as follows:
Millions
1943		 $1,149,232,444
1944		 1,301,322,402
1945		 1,196,976,726
The difference between the exports and the imports, the unfavourable balance of trade, in each case was as follows:
1943		 $274,404,042
1944		 145,903,513
1945		 5,440,908
I raise this question of privilege only because the accuracy of the figures I was quoting was questioned by the minister, and I wanted to explain that the figures were taken from a government document.

subtopic: MR. BRACKEN-REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON DECEMBER 9

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), the adjournment of the house under standing order 31, for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely, the plight of war veterans and their dependents due to the government's failure to increase the basic rates of pensions and allowances to meet the high cost of living, with the result that the pensioners and recipients of war veterans allowances are suffering extreme hardship and are unable to obtain in full the ordinary necessities of life.
I am sure it must be perfectly obvious to you, Mr. Speaker, and to every member of this house and the people as a whole that this is a very urgent matter as far as pensioners and war veterans are concerned, and I would point out that there has been no opportunity since this session commenced, nor will there be an opportunity, to discuss this matter.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):

subtopic: QUESTION OF PROCEDURE-PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS
speechtext: His Honour the Speaker has called orders of the day. I wish to make a brief statement on the orders of the day.

speechtext:

the order in which the routine proceedings are printed, some hon. members apparently assume that the first order will be questions, and that the next will be notices of motions. That is not in accordance with the motion the house carried on Monday last which gave precedence to government orders.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: QUESTION OF PROCEDURE-PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS
speechtext:
So that today we proceed under orders of the day, with government orders, the first order to be called being:
Resuming the adjourned debate on the motion of the Prime Minister: That it is expedient that parliament do approve the general agreement on tariffs and trade . . .

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: QUESTION OF PROCEDURE-PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS
speechtext:
I rise to a point of order with respect to the procedure now being followed. We have before us an order paper which says that the next, item, on page 3,

is "Questions". I hold in my hand copies of a number of order papers of last session. These are order papers for days when the ordinary procedure of the house under standing order 15 had been altered. Every time the procedure was altered by a decision of the house, that alteration was reflected in a change in the order paper. Inasmuch as today's order paper has not been changed to conform with what the Prime Minister says was the interpretation of Monday's resolution, I submit we should follow the order paper as it is. I shall not take the time to quote from these order papers of last year, but that was the case when the debate on the speech from the throne was a special order. Then a little later the debate on the speech from the throne was suspended so we could deal with the control bill, and the special order was put into the latter part of the order paper. Later in the session, when we dispensed with Monday as a private members day-for example, here is Monday, June 23-private members resolutions were placed at the latter part of the order paper.
I submit that if the motion passed on Monday governs today, which I challenge, it should have been reflected in the order paper. That not having been done, I submit that we should follow the order paper that is before us. Otherwise what is the use of an order paper anyway?

subtopic: QUESTION OF PROCEDURE-PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this was a point of order which I intended to raise myself. The Prime Minister has said that he consulted with the Clerk of the House, but I regret to say that I am unable to accept his interpretation of the effect of the resolution which was passed on Monday. I submit that that decision should come from Your Honour. Supporting as I do the view put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), I ask for your ruling on the question whether or not the resolution passed on Monday was not confined exclusively to that day. The resolution is to be found on page 40 of Votes and Proceedings, and it is qualified by the Prime Minister so that it applied only to December 8th instant. There was nothing in that resolution which could be taken to govern proceedings on subsequent days. The resolution reads:
That the debate on the address in reply to the speech of His Excellency the Governor General to both houses of parliament be the first order of business on Monday, December 8th instant, and that this order be followed by government notices of motion and government orders notwithstanding anything in standing order 15.
I submit that the inclusion of the words "Monday, December 8th instant," without

Business oj the House
any subsequent qualification, means that the effect of the motion was to be confined exclusively to that day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: QUESTION OF PROCEDURE-PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS
speechtext: If I may have an opportunity to speak now, I should like to do so.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: QUESTION OF PROCEDURE-PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS
speechtext: Are you speaking to the point of order?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: QUESTION OF PROCEDURE-PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS
speechtext: I am trying to answer my hon. friend, yes. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has drawn attention to what was done last year with respect to the order of business. If I recall aright, what was done last year was done under a motion similar to one that I had in mind making at one stage of our proceedings but which did not come before the house. That motion provided that on and after a certain day government notices of motion and government orders would have precedence over all other business except the introduction of bills, questions of members and notices of motion for the production of papers. A motion similar to that has not been carried at this session, and it was not carried-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: QUESTION OF PROCEDURE-PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS
speechtext: That is the whole point.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: QUESTION OF PROCEDURE-PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS
speechtext:
-because some hon. gentlemen opposite insisted on the first motion I presented being discussed and voted upon without the deletion of any part of it. It will be recalled I was prepared to delete the first two lines beginning, "and that this order be followed", etc. The motion as passed read:
That the debate on the address in reply to the speech of His Excellency the Governor General to both houses of parliament be the first order of business on Monday, December 8th instant, and that this order be followed by government notices of motion and government orders notwithstanding anything in standing order 15.
Standing order 15 sets forth the routine of the business of the house for each day in the [DOT]week. This motion distinctly supersedes any procedure set out in standing order 15.

subtopic: QUESTION OF PROCEDURE-PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS
speechtext: But only for Monday, December 8.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: QUESTION OF PROCEDURE-PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS
speechtext: That was only for Monday, December 8.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: QUESTION OF PROCEDURE-PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS
speechtext: I do not agree with my hon. friend. I made that clear on two occasions, and exception was not taken *by my hon. friend until this moment.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: QUESTION OF PROCEDURE-PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS
speechtext: Oh, yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: QUESTION OF PROCEDURE-PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS
speechtext:
If I may so describe it, I cannot understand why hon. gentlemen are making a mountain out of a molehill. The object of this session is to get on with certain specified measures. The government is adopting the procedure which it believes will enable the house to get on with that work rapidly. The house has given the government authority to proceed in a certain way notwithstanding anything in standing order 15. The fact that the order paper has been printed in a certain sequence by those who have to do with the printing does not alter in the least the authority which the government has been given under the order which this house has passed. I say to my hon. friend that like other hon. members of the house I was surprised when I saw all these questions and notices of motions printed in advance of government notices of motions and government orders in today's order paper. I immediately went to the Clerk and asked how it was that this order paper came to be printed in that way, knowing that the Clerk had agreed with me before, as I have stated in the house, that under the motion adopted by the house on Monday last government notices of motions and government orders would have precedence over everything else. The Clerk informed me that this was a matter of technical procedure; that notwithstanding what the house had passed, questions and notices of motions were therefore retained on the order paper in the order in which they appear today, but that notwithstanding, the rules which would govern the house and its procedure today would be those which were in accord with the motion the house had passed on Monday last.
What I am anxious to do is to have the house get on with its business. Are my hon. friends insisting at the moment that we should take up questions now and then notices of motions?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: QUESTION OF PROCEDURE-PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS
speechtext: We are only asking that it be done in the proper way. If the Prime Minister had asked for unanimous consent for the passing of his second motion on Monday, as we think should have been done, there would have been none of this trouble.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: QUESTION OF PROCEDURE-PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS
speechtext: I wish I had the same faith in what this house is prepared to do in the matter of giving unanimous consent as the hon. member has.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: QUESTION OF PROCEDURE-PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS
speechtext: You can get it right now if you ask for it; all we want is to have the rules followed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: QUESTION OF PROCEDURE-PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS
speechtext:
From what has taken place this week, I have come to the

Business of the House

conclusion that no matter what the government proposes it will not get unanimous consent, that that is a deliberate policy of some hon. gentlemen opposite. The only way I see in which matters of procedure can be met is for the government to decide what the procedure shall be, and when that procedure has been approved by the house, then act upon it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: QUESTION OF PROCEDURE-PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS
speechtext: Do it in the proper way.

subtopic: QUESTION OF PROCEDURE-PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS
speechtext:
Speaking to the point of order, what the Prime Minister has said with regard to unanimous consent does not apply to this group. We are very anxious to get along with what the house was called here to do, and we have shown every disposition to help the government in the matter. But we are not going to agree to the rules of the house being set aside simply because the Clerk or anyone else says so.
I should like to draw the attention of the Prime Minister and the house to the situation that existed last Monday. On Monday there were two resolutions on the order paper under the name of the Prime Minister. One of them had to do with the procedure for Monday, December 8-and it clearly stated Monday, December 8. Then if we finished with the debate on the address on that day, if the various leaders and certain others spoke, we were to go on to government notices of motion and government orders. That that is what the Prime Minister had in mind when he put that motion on the order paper is *shown clearly by the next motion, which uealt with business on Tuesday and every day thereafter. All we want the Prime Minister to do is to abide by that resolution dealing with Tuesday and the following days. Then we will do everything in our power to give him unanimous consent.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: QUESTION OF PROCEDURE-PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS
speechtext: We will vote for it.

subtopic: QUESTION OF PROCEDURE-PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS
speechtext: Yes, we will vote for it. We believe that he has adopted a procedure that is contrary to the procedure of this house. In all the time that I have been here I have never seen an occasion on which the order paper has not reflected the order of business that would come up, because in no other way can the members of the house know what business is going to come up. They have to follow the order paper. If the Prime Minister is simply to turn to such and such an item on page 12 of the order paper, page 16 or any other page, we shall have no control over our procedure at all, I submit that the Prime Minister should ask for unanimous consent to put this resolution and get the matter straightened out so that we may proceed in an orderly manner.

subtopic: QUESTION OF PROCEDURE-PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS
speechtext:
The motion on which the point of order has been raised by the hon. member reads:
That the debate on the address in reply to the speech of His Excellency the Governor General to both houses of parliament be the first order of business on Monday, December 8th instant, and that this order be followed by government notices of motion and government orders, notwithstanding anything in standing order 15.
According to this motion, which has been carried by the house, I believe that I should now call government orders. Orders of the day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947 -NOTICE OF AMENDMENT OF RESOLUTION

speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, December 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie King:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve the general agreement on tariffs and trade, including the protocol of provisional ap-
Tariffs and Trade

plication thereof, annexed to the final act of the second session of the preparatory committee of the united nations conference on trade and employment held at Geneva from April 10 to October 30, 1947, together with the complementary agreements of October 30, 1947, between Canada and the United States of America and between Canada and the United Kingdom; and that this house do approve of the same, subject to the legislation required in order to give effect to the provisions thereof.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
and seventy per cent are subject to tariff reductions. Even more impressive, nearly sixty per cent of our dutiable exports as of 1939 will be entitled to tariff reductions of from thirty-six per cent to fifty per cent from present levels. In other words practically the entire range of American tariff restrictions against Canadian goods has been reviewed and very substantially reduced. Furthermore, in general the largest tariff reductions will apply to those exports that are already entering the United States on a competitive basis in spite of the present tariff restrictions. The reductions the United States has made therefore have substance. It will be up to us to take full advantage of the opportunities presented.
I have confidence that Canadian farmers and business men will take advantage of the new trade outlets afforded as quickly as supplies will allow, and that Canadian resources, management and labour will produce the goods for export.
In return Canada has granted concessions of importance, both directly and indirectly, to the United States. In direct tariff reductions it would not appear that we have gone as far as the United States did. In terms ol 1939 trade ninety per cent of our exports to the United States are affected, while we propose tariff reductions or bound rates on seventy per cent of our imports from that country. 'As compared with reductions by the United States on seventy per cent of the dutiable imports received from us, we propose to make reductions on forty-five per cent of the dutiable imports from them. Finally, while most * of the United States tariff reductions will range from 36 per cent to 50 per cent, the majority of our reductions of rates on American imports will range from 15 per cent to 20 per cent.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext: Very misleading.

speechtext:

Some lion. MEMBERS: Oh, oh.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I like to agree with a Tory occasionally. These comparisons, however, must be qualified. Reductions given by us to other countries will apply to the United

States on a most-favoured-nation basis. Second, a higher proportion of American exports to Canada are dutiable than of Canadian exports to the United States, and the proportion has grown since 1939. Third, the general level of tariffs is lower in Canada than in the United States, so that a moderate reduction in our tariff on some commodity is often more significant than a larger reduction in the United States tariff. Finally an important concession was made by reducing or eliminating the margin of British preference on a number of items.
Coming now to the trade between Canada and the United Kingdom, the United Kingdom and other members of the British commonwealth joined with Canada in reducing the margin of British preference. The Prime Minister has already outlined the history of the British preference in our tariff structure and the position we took on this matter at Geneva. We had, of course, a twofold interest: preferences enjoyed by Canada in other parts of the commonwealth and preferences granted by Canada to other commonwealth countries. These preferences which we gave up in other parts of the commonwealth were given up in return for tariff concessions we had from the United States. These preferences granted by us which were reduced were reduced with the consent of the other countries of the commonwealth which were affected. The United Kingdom report on the Geneva tariff negotiations puts it in this way:
In so far as the reduction or elimination of these preferences affects the United Kingdom, the United Kingdom has secured due compensation in its negotiations for tariff concessions from the foreign country or countries primarily interested, or. alternatively, the United Kingdom has accepted in exchange tariff concessions from the commonwealth country according the preferences, and has thus enabled the latter to claim credit from the foreign country, or countries, primarily interested.
The reasons for the modifications made in the preferences can be put very simply. In the first place there would have been no Geneva agreement had the commonwealth countries not agreed to some reductions in their mutual margins of preference. In the second place all commonwealth countries, including ourselves, were faced with dollar problems, and the preference reductions were in direct exchange for concessions from non-commonwealth countries that offered an opportunity to earn more dollars.
It should be pointed out that while a number of preference margins have been reduced, there have also been many tariff reductions made between commonwealth countries at Geneva, and the volume of trade between common-

Tariffs and Trade
wealth countries should rise. The system of commonwealth preferences has been modified but not abandoned. This can be demonstrated by analysing the effect of changes in our preferential tariffs on imports coming from the United Kingdom in 1938. In that year nearly $200,000,000 of imports were brought into Canada from the United Kingdom, of which about eighty per cent enjoyed preference guarantees. The changes it is proposed to make under the Geneva agreement would affect about 830.000,000 of this trade by lowering or eliminating preferential rates. In other words approximately 58 per cent of the 1938 imports from Great Britain would have been unaffected, because they did not come wfithin the system of preferences. Another 26 per cent would be unaffected though subject to preference guarantees. That is a total of 84 per cent, and the remaining 16 per cent is divided up as follows: about 4 per cent with the same rates as before but minus their preference guarantees; about 8 per cent with rates lowered as much as 35 per cent, and about 4 per cent placed on a duty free basis. The 193S imports that W'ould have lost preferential treatment would be valued at about $13,000,000. This is about seven per cent of the total imports from the United Kingdom or 16 per cent of the imports with preference guarantees. Clearly the system of preferences has not been abandoned.
What will be the effect of all this on Canadian industries? In summary, we have reduced or bound tariffs on about two-thirds of our imports, and in return we have received concessions on about three-quarters of our present exports. As I previously mentioned, of particular importance in view of our current exchange difficulties is that seventy per cent of our dutiable exports to the United States will benefit from tariff reductions ranging in most cases from a third to a half. I think it would be of interest to review briefly some of the implications of these reductions in United States tariffs for the major Canadian industries.
First I should like to discuss agriculture. Virtually the complete range of our agricultural exports to the United States have been accorded tariff reductions, in most cases the maximum of fifty per cent. The most important items are wheat, oats, barley, rye, mill-feeds, screenings, alfalfa, clover and other forage seeds; beef, veal and poultry; butter and eggs, milk and cream, and cheese; seed potatoes, turnips, and other vegetables and fruits. In other words the duty into the United States on those commodities has been cut in half.

speechtext: Has the minister figures to show what the average duty was before the cut?

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
That information will appear as we proceed.
In addition the quota on cattle has been raised from 225,000 head to 400.000 head. I am told that 400,000 head of cattle per annum is the maximum this country could possibly ship to the United States in any one year. The quota on calves is raised from 100,000 to
200,000.	The list of Canadian concessions is as extensive, since the principle was generally followed of granting reciprocal rates, but the substance of the agreement is obviously in the greatly improved competitive position in *which a number of Canada's most important agricultural products are put.
Since most of the United States duties on agricultural products are specific, the higher current price level combines with the rate reductions to lower the effective incidence of the tariff. For example, the former 42 cents United States duty on a bushel of wheat was just about the price many prairie farmers received in the thirties; the new 21-cent rate is less than 10 per cent of the current world price.	.
I was most .amazed last night to hear the leader of the opposition ('Mr. Bracken), who has lived almost all his life in western Canada and is an expert in farming, say that the reduction of the duty on wheat to 21 cents a bushel would not be beneficial to the farmers. The rate of 21 cents is less than the freight rate to Fort William from some parts of Canada.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext: What would the benefit be?

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext: The benefit would be that a seller of wheat could take advantage of the United States market.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT

speechtext: Nevertheless, as hon. members know, today our wheat is under contract to Great Britain and permission is not given to ship across the boundary. But if permission were given, it would permit the Canadian farmer to get for his wheat on the open market the United States price, less 21 cents a bushel.

speechtext: Will the minister say if wheat is to be permitted to pass over the United States border?

speechtext:
That depends entirely upon the length 6f time in which we feel obligated to deliver our wheat to the United Kingdom. So long as o.ur British agreement stands, only our surplus above contract requirements can be shipped to the United States.
Tariffs and Trade

Similarly the new duties on oats of 4 cents a bushel, on barley of 71 cents, and on rye of 6 cents d-o not form serious barriers today. The halving of the former 6 cents a pound rate on beef and veal restores us to the position of 1927 when we exported over 50 million pounds.
Combined with the increased quota on cattle and the 50 per cent reduction in rates on edible offal, the Canadian livestock and associated industries stand to benefit materially. The principle of reciprocal tariff rates, applied pretty well across the board, should lead to a substantial development of localized border exchange in both directions, to mutual advantage. While our present contract commitments to the United Kingdom may prevent Canada from taking immediate advantage of this changed situation, it is obvious that the future security and prosperity of Canadian agriculture has been greatly strengthened.
Turning now to fisheries products, Canada has obtained concessions from the United States on virtually all kinds of fish, both fresh water and salt water, and in all forms, whether fresh, frozen, dried, smoked or canned.

speechtext: Not on canned salmon?

speechtext: No reduction at all.

speechtext: No reduction at all.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I think you will find the explanation for that from your own fishing industry.
Most of the tariff reductions have been the 50 per cent maximum. It should also be mentioned that some advantageous adjustments were made in the tariffs of other important markets, such as Cuba and Brazil.
Probably the most important single item is the binding of the existing United States 2J cents per pound duty on fresh or frozen fillets of cod, haddock, and some other fish, which applies to all imports in excess of the existing quota. I might point out that the existing quota is 15 per cent of United States consumption. The quota goes in at a lower rate, but the battle was to bind the pound rate on the fish shipped in in excess of the quota. Our negotiators had to fight long and hard for this, and it protects a promising and expanding market. In addition, some changes in the administration of the United States quota are provided for, which will help to protect our fishermen's interests in competition with Newfoundland, Iceland and Norway.

Turning next to forest products, significant concessions were obtained for this industry, which is third in importance in Canada's primary industries, only surpassed by agriculture and mining, We have gained concessions for 90 per cent of our forest products exports, which in 1946 amounted to $626 million.
The most important concession was a 50 per cent cut covering both the duty and internal revenue code tax on softwoods. For pine, spruce, hemlock, fir and birch the combined rate, that is the duty and the I.R.C. tax, was reduced from $2 to $1 per thousand board feet.
There are great potentialities for Canadian exports of softwood lumber to the United States for many years to come. In 1916 the United States consumed some 26 billion board feet with only five per cent of this requirement met by imports, of which Canada supplied about 95 per cent. As long as a high level of economic activity continues in the United States, lumber requirements are likely to be even greater than the 1946 volume- possibly 25 per cent higher. Export restr'e-tions have been eased, and the Canadian softwood lumber industry should be in a position to expand its United States market.
Numerous concessions were obtained on wood products. I mention only one which may have particular meaning for our veneer and plywood manufacturers. The duty on veneers of all types of wood is now down to 10 per cent ad valorem. The old rate for all but birch and maple has been 20 per cent. Red cedar plywood is down from 40 per cent to 20 per cent. During the war we made great strides in the production of plywood and veneers. We all remember the miracle of the Mosquito bombers, which was made possible through the specially developed techniques of producing and treating plywood.
I believe we are today as efficient in the production of these commodities as any other country in the world. I am sure the industry will welcome the opportunity to prove its competitiveness in foreign markets which are now opening up.
An important segment of our forestry industry is the pulp and paper industry. The Geneva trade agreements have assured us of continuing duty-free exports to the United States of newsprint and pulpwood. In 1946 these two items brought us a quarter of a billion in United States currency, and American needs are rising further.
With reference to mineral products, about 85 per cent of our important base metal exports, and nearly 60 per cent of our non-

Tariffs and Trade
metallic, and related product exports, will receive concessions. Of these the most important are copper and zinc, on which reductions are approximately 50 per cent, and aluminum, where the three cent duty is reduced to two cents a pound. No action has been taken on lead, pending negotiations by the United States with Mexico. In addition, reductions on ferro-alloys, a number of non-ferrous metals such as magnesium, tantalum and cadmium, and a wide range of industrially important non-metallics such as cement, crushed stone refractories, and feldspar, should be mentioned.
These changes are of particular significance to us since they confirm a trend which has been evident for some time. As the mineral reserves of the United States are diminished, it was logical that attention will turn increasingly to Canadian mineral and associated hydro power resources. The new tariff rates are a great step forward in achieving an economic integration of North American resources, to the mutual advantage of the northern and southern halves, and they should have some immediately stimulating and expansive effects in Canada.
The various commodity groups I have mentioned contain many manufactured goods. Three other commodity groups I have not mentioned-iron and its products, chemicals and related products, and textiles and textile products-are overwhelmingly manufactured goods. In fact three-quarters of all our exports are now fully or partly processed. It is on the manufacturing industries, in particular, that we must depend to extend our markets abroad, and more specifically to extend them in the dollar area. For this reason I wish to draw the attention of this house to the increased productive capacity and export potential of our manufacturing industries.
During six years of war many Canadian manufacturing industries underwent marked expansion; some relatively small industries were expanded to an extent that it was tantamount to the creation of new industries, such as aircraft and shipbuilding; and new industries were created, as for example roller bearings, magnesium and artificial rubber. In this process of growth many new types of goods were produced, such as optical glass, high octane gasoline, penicillin and sulpha drugs. In the two years that have followed the war most of these wartime gains have been consolidated and further advances made in a large number of fields. We are now producing at least 200 items never before made in Canada, ranging from scientific instruments bo special types
of pulp-mill machinery, from cordless electric irons to diesel engines, from precision instruments to road building equipment, from plywood furniture to prefabricated houses.
What this industrial development means in terms of export potential has been amply demonstrated from a study of applications for special rates of depreciation under the Income War Tax Act. A sample of some 2,250 companies indicated that they exported $325 million worth of goods in 1939, $670 million in 1944, and that they expected to be able to export $1-2 billion after completion of their modernization and expansion projects. This means exports about three and one-half times as much in value terms, or two and one-half times in volume terms, as before the war.
As a result of the many concessions obtained on manufactured products under the Geneva agreement, potential markets have been opened in many directions. In particular two industries that in pre-war days were relatively unimportant and that enjoyed marked expansion during the war stand to benefit. These are the secondary iron and steel industry and the chemical industry. Over 80 per cent of our chemical and allied exports receive concessions under the trade pacts. The United States also granted the maximum reduction on the entire range of metal articles and metal wares of from 45 per cent to 22$ per cent. On the "basket" item of machinery, "not elsewhere specified", which includes a great variety of Rems, the rate has been reduced from 27$ per cent to 15 per cent.
I have had first hand opportunity during the war to observe the growth of our tool making and metal products and parts manufacturing industries. Canadian manufacturers proved often just as efficient as their American competitors and, given large scale production, were in a great many instances able to manufacture goods of the same quality, but at lower costs than in the United States. Proximity, an ample supply of natural resources, and cheap power, were important factors.
I shall give you just a few instances of the possibilities which Canadian manufacturers believe could be developed, based on representations made for the information of our delegates at Geneva. Before the war Canada had exported hardly any auto trailers, but one company has been able to convert its war establishment to the peacetime production of auto trailers at costs which compare favourably with similar products manufactured in the United States. This company alone hoped to achieve exports up to $3 million per year if a tariff reduction could be obtained. The rate
i36
Tariffs and Trade

was cut by 50 per cent. Another Canadian company thought it could work up exports of
81,000,000 worth of canned peas if the United States rates were brought down to the Canadian rate. The duties in both countries were equalized. Producers of specialized equipment, where Canada is particularly proficient, as for example in the manufacture of sports equipment, submitted that they could considerably increase their exports to the United States if the duty was cut. Duties on equipment for exercise and play were reduced by 50 per cent, from the former level of 30 per cent down to 15 per cent. Another company was producing specialized steel bars. It thought it could develop substantial exports to the United States if some tariff adjustment were made. The rate for such bars was reduced by 50 per rent. Another firm was producing an important industrial chemical, acetic acid, more cheaply than it was produced in the United States. This was possible because of the convenient availability of most of the raw materials required and of cheap hydro power. While an export trade had been successfully developed in the past, the company felt that it could substantially expand sales to the United States if existing tariff barriers could be overcome. The tariff rates for this commodity were substantially reduced, from between 25 and 50 per cent.
These are only a few instances. Many other opportunities are opening up, as Canadian manufacturing industries are studying the implications of the tariff reductions of the Geneva agreement for their own business, and are discovering that they will now be able to enter United States markets on more competitive grounds than was the case before. We can rely on Canadian industry, which has grown so rapidly in stature during the last eight years, to make the best of these opportunities.
I have dealt almost exclusively with the tariff adjustments made by other countries, and particularly the United States, which will provide an opportunity for Canada to expand export markets. The reason for this is, of course, obviods; it arises from our United! States dollar shortage. Most of the concessions which we have undertaken to give on imports will of necessity be inoperative for a period owing to the exchange restrictions which we have been required to impose. As I indicated earlier, article XII of the Geneva agreement specifically recognizes our right to take such action when necessary to correct serious balance of payments difficulties.
At first glance it appears contradictory that we are proceeding simultaneously with the Geneva trade agreement and our conservation of exchange measures. One is an expansive

policy and the other, for the time being, must be restrictive. The two policies, however, are balanced and complementary. It is by virtue of developments made possible by the Geneva agreement-and we hope further agreements along the same line-that our present dollar shortage will be overcome.
In looking at Canadian-American trade in the past we see that whenever Canada has been prosperous, our adverse balance of payments with the United States has grown, and that it has only approached a more equal balance in periods of depression and low income in Canada. We are now forced by the United States dollar shortage of our chief overseas customers to find ways and means of achieving a more even and stable balance in our trade with the United States.
One way is to achieve a balance at a low level of trade, as has been done in the past, when Canadian industrial activity was at such a low ebb, and Canadian incomes were so reduced, that our purchases from the United States fell even more drastically than our sales to them. The alternative way and, I need scarcely add, the way that accords with this government's fundamental views on trade, is to achieve the balance at a high level, by our selling more. Even our import controls will be administered to contribute to this end; imports of capital goods for non-essential construction will be drastically curtailed, but imports which will contribute to the development of the Canadian economy, the expansion of our export trade, and the conservation and production of exchange, will have high priority.
It is a fortunate coincidence that at the same time we are faced with a critical balance of paj'ments situation, agreement should have been reached, across such a broad front, with the other chief trading nations of the world on practical ways and means of expanding trade. It is to constructive and expansive development in Canada, stimulated by these agreements, that we look for a permanent and satisfactory solution of our chronic dollar shortage, a solution which will not be at the expense of Canadian living standards and incomes but which will, in the long run, fortify and develop both.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have just listened
to a very interesting speech by the right hon. Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) upon the schedule to this agreement dealing with the tariff items. Toward the end of his remarks he made a significant statement "which I think he or some other member of the government should explain to the house in more detail as soon as possible. He said that it was the intention of the government to

Tariffs and Trade
balance our trade with the United States on a high level, instead of a low level. That is a very interesting statement and a very good aim. But in view of the figures put upon the record last night by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken), I should like the minister to take the first opportunity of telling us just how he is going to bring about that monumental achievement. We have never before, in all our history, -been able to achieve balance with the United States of America.
Before I go further, Mr. Speaker, I would draw to your attention that this debate is getting off the track once more. The right hon. gentleman, in an endeavour to sugar-coat the government's restriclion piogram, has given us a great speech in which he hardly mentioned at all the subject of the resolution before us. He mentioned only the tariff concessions, which are the subject of a totally different resolution. So we have gone today from page 14 to page 12 of the order paper. On the resolution before us we should not be discussing at all schedule V of the agreement dealing with the reduction of tariffs. What the right hon. gentlemen should have been doing was explaining to the house the meaning of the main agreement. While the tariff items are -bound for three years, and are subject, of course, to renegotiation, the main agreement is a document from which, if we accept it, we shall not wish to withdraw at any time. It will be our desire once we accept it, to carry out its provisions loyally, and that is why the right hon. gentleman should have explained it to the house.
So that we may get this discussion into a little better order and stick to the resolution we are dealing with, instead of straying to other resolutions, I now move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green):
That this house is of the opinion that the said resolution should be referred to the committee of the whole house, with instructions to divide the subject matter thereof between -two resolutions, one relating to the general agreement on tariffs and trade and the complementary agreement between Canada and the United States, and the other relating to the agreement respecting preferential tariffs between Canada and the United Kingdom.
This amendment, Mr. Speaker, 'places formally before the house what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) agreed to earlier this afternoon and what we certainly had intended to insist upon, as we consider it to be of the utmost importance.
Unlike the Minister of Reconstruction, restricting myself to the resolution before us I want, first, to comment on what was said 5849-10
last night by the Prime Minister when he placed the agreement before the house. I, like other hon. members, I suppose, approached this international agreement between twenty-three nations with a sort of holy awe. I imagine we all thought it was the result of a great effort of the united nations to get together to show the way toward wider trade. I think we all probably had a wish to approve the agreement and no great desire to criticize it, except for our duty to criticize where we thought it was wrong. I think, too, we all had a great good will particularly toward the eight signatories of the protocol who intend to bring the agreement into effect on the first of January, because, after all, those eight nations, of which we are one, are friends, and one has always great good will toward one's friends.
But last night the Prime Minister brought this discussion down to a narrow and bitter partisan statement, not of the merits of wider trade throughout the world, not of the great things that were accomplished at this meeting of twenty-three nations, but a violent statement of old Liberal doctrinaire free trade, accompanied by an attack on the tariff pol-'icies of the party to which I have the honour to belong, which policies the Prime Minister has always criticized but has ever practised. I do not think it became the right hon. gentleman to introduce the agreement in that spirit, and it certainly relieved me of any awe or respect that I held toward this agreement. If it is to be the plaything of Liberal propaganda we shall all be free to attack it, and that is what the Prime Minister made it.
The Prime Minister also criticized the Ottawa trade agreements. The Ottawa trade agreements were come to in this country as a result of another unfavourable trade balance built up by the government of the right hon. gentleman, as the leader of the opposition pointed out last night. Whatever the right hon. gentleman may have thought of the empire agreements, which he and his whole party opposed so bitterly in 1932, there is no doubt that, had it not been for those agreements, the great timber industry in British Columbia and many great manufacturing industries across this country would not be there for the Minister of Reconstruction to tinker with as he is doing today.
I also wish to say to the Prime Minister that if he did not agree with the Ottawa agreements as a way to get out of the difficulties which he himself was not able to solve in the spring of 1930; if he did not agree wit-h that method of making long-term trade deals with one's friends, then at least such methods are better than the totalitarian ideae
Tariffs and Tra.de

which he is about to introduce in the next fe\v days, and w'hich he is trying to hide behind these present agreements.
I wish to say to him as well that, no matter what he might say now, no matter how he may consent to amendments to these resolutions, he rushed these agreements into the house. It was his intention, as appears from the order paper, and as appeared yesterday up to the time he heard the views of the leaders of the opposition parties upon it, that, these agreements should be given a cursory examination and voted on without going to a committee and being examined by bon. members. It is all very well for him to say, and for the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply to intervene in. the debate last night and say, that there had been reconsideration, and that the government was prepared to let these agreements go to the committee. But I could not help thinking that in regard to "escape clauses" which we heard discussed for a short time last night, the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply himself was an ambulatory escape clause for the government.
Last night when either the Prime Minister or the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply mentioned the fact that these agreements would probably be modified at Havana, I wondered why the necessity for bringing them to the house now and asking us to approve them. It seems to me that is another example of an attempt to treat this parliament as a rubber-stamp for anything agreed to by the government. Why was that done? There is no question about it. It is perfectly clear from what has gone on throughout this session that these agreements are here before us now, not with the idea of our giving them a satisfactory examination, but only so that a red herring may be dragged across the path and the Canadian people fooled into thinking that these agreements are going to guide our ways in the next few years instead of the restrictions which have already been imposed1 upon us.
In attempting to use this agreement as a cloak for the other measures, the Prime Minister was being fairer to his party than to the country. These agreements are not just formal matters to be brushed awray lightly. They contain new principles upon which international trade is to be founded. They will change or they could change everything we have known in international trade over the years. They can change what has been Canada's settled policy since confederation, and they should be examined very, very carefully and very, very closely, not only by a committee of this house, but also by the country at large. We may then get some

general idea, not only of how world trade is affected, but also how Canada itself is affected by the agreement.
The practical effect of these agreements upon the economy and the whole future of this nation may be very great indeed. They may affect our power to control our levels of employment, our standard of living and even the political alignments we have always had with other countries of the world. All these things follow trends of trade just as trends of trade follow political and social thought as well as economic thought.
I would not have expected from the Prime Minister a Liberal propaganda speech; I would have expected from him an explanation of what the consequences of these agreements were likely to be to Canada, because it is Canada which will be chiefly affected by these agreements so far as this parliament is concerned. I would not have thought we would have been given the momentary and immediate effects of the tariff concessions; I would have thought the whole future of Canada was bound up in this main agreement and we should think of it with an eye to our future as a nation. I hold in my hand the Whaley-Eaton news-letter of November 18, 1947, which probably most hon. members have had in front of them. I wish to read from paragraph 8, which is headed "Canada". It reads as follows:
This week has also seen a trade development in many ways transcending the foregoing in importance. While the press concentrates on Canada's luxury-import restrictions, virtually overlooked. because unannounced, is the fact that economic fusion between Canada and the United States is being negotiated.
I skip the bit about the export-import bank loan because the Minister of Finance has denied it, and I come to this:
Also, in consequence, Canada would tailor her whole production in such manner as to supplement that of the United States; as far as could be achieved without damage to the immediate needs of Europe's recovery, she would concentrate her agriculture, mining and industry on the chinks in America's productive armour. "This is a super-Hvdc Park agreement"; and an authoritative comment is that, if this should raise difficulties over the U.N.-ITO concept (most-favoured-nation, etc., etc.), a way of reconciliation could be found.
That is a very blunt statement and is expressed as if the negotiations are now a fact, and that these negotiations are going on. It is not only this United States publication which has set the rumour going or sounded the warning. It appears also in a more modified form in the Financial Post and has appeared in several publications over the past two or three months as a possible solution of our

Tariffs and Trade
problem. I would have thought the Prime Minister would take the opportunity to tell the country if anything is going on in that direction and if, in fact, something like that is happening, what he sees to 'be Canada's future as a result of the new' alignment. I think there are many people in Canada who would be most interested to know whether there is any foundation whatever for reports like these.
When I hear the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply say, as he did a moment ago, that these trade agreements will lead to a greater economic integration of the north and south, I want to know what that means, and I think there are a lot of people in Canada who also want to know.
With some of these ideas in mind, I wish to examine, not the schedule, but the agreement itself, and I am going to examine it critically because I think it is our duty to do just that. I think it is our duty to find out what this means, not in terms of world trade, but in terms of its effect on Canada itself. It may be that the criticisms which I shall make will be overcome in my mind, and I shall be very happy if that can be done. But I think the criticism should be made in this house and an answer be given by the government upon it.
Confining myself to the agreement only, and not referring to the tariff schedule or exchange of notes on preferences, I say that this agreement is intended to be a permanent document. It is, of course, possible for any country to withdraw from it at the end of three years, on giving six months' notice. But that is not the intention, and it would not be Canada's intention if we went into it. It is intended to be permanent, and I think it is intended principally to be an agreement whereby nations forbear regulation of external trade save by way of tariffs. If it stopped there I think it would be good; I think it would be splendid. But it does not stop there. It goes on to import, not a principle of wider trade, but a principle of non-discrimination, and it assumes that non-discrimination between nations will bring about wider trade. I am not here to say whether that is right or wrong. I do not think there is any one among us who can say whether non-discrimination between all nations signatory to this pact will bring about wider trade, because that has never been tried before. We are breaking completely new ground when we accept that principle as one which will lead us to wider trade.
Let us examine a little more closely the principle of non-discrimination. I like it at first. It has a nice sound. I do not like dis-5849-10i
criminating against anyone. I am not so certain that, in many cases, one would not be justified in discriminating in favour of people. I am not so certain either that discrimination in favour of people is an evil thing. I think it might often be a good thing. I think it might often be a necessary thing. No matter how high our ideals might foe for the world, I am afraid that discrimination in favour of people might be a necessary thing.
But let us see what it means. First, the agreement says that Canada can not discriminate in tariffs between other nations; that is the most-favoured-nation clause. What is given to one must go to all. Is that a sound principle, Mr. Speaker, upon which to base our international trade for all time to come? Certainly it means the end of preferences. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, in his speech just a few minutes ago, said that there wouldi have been no Genera agreements at all if the preferential system had not been breached. I think the logical application of the principle of non-discrimination must be eventually the end of empire preferences. That seems to me one result of the application of this principle.
Let me examine for a moment more whether this principle is sound.
It would be sound between countries which are equal at the start. Between soldiers in the ranks we do not discriminate. They all wear the same uniform; they are all equal. But unfortunately the nations of the world are not all equal. There is the United States, a great country with great national resources, a great population and now at the height of her great industrial power. There is Great Britain, a small country with a large population, with great industrialization, but whose natural resources are greatly diminished and not as rich as those of the other country I mentioned. There is Norway, a country which depends greatly upon her forest industry and her shipping industry, which has a small population aud has her place in a northern clime. There is China, a huge nation with
400,000,000 people or thereabouts, with a low standard of living, different educational standards, and no great industrialization. There is Canada, a nation on her way up, a nation which is going on to a great future, but which has a great deal of development to do, as the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply very-well knows, before she will reach her great, position in this world.
These nations are all different in every way; the economy of one nation is complementary to that of another, while it is competitive to that of a third. These are differences which we have been unable to avoid in the past.
Tariffs and Trade

We have never before been able to practise non-discrimination in trade. If we have a surplus product in the future, under article I of this agreement we shall no longer be able to make a discriminatory concession to a country that wants to take our surplus product, unless we give that concession to another country that does not want to take our surplus product. If we want to discriminate in favour of a country which owes us money, so that her goods can come in free and so nelp to balance the terms of trade, we shall be unable to do that without making similar concessions to other nations.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext: Thank God for that.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply says: "Thank God for that". It may be so. I simply want to bring this matter to the attention of the house and to suggest, for instance, that what the government is doing right now, namely, lowering the tariff against Great Britain under the War Exchange Conservation Act, we shall not be able to go on doing if this agreement is adopted' by Canada.
So much for discrimination between outside nations. Here is another angle of non-discrimination that I never realized before I read this agreement. We shall not be able to discriminate in favour of ourselves. We shall not be able to discriminate in favour of our own home-produced goods in our own country, which goods are not exported to other parts of the world. I want to give the house a few examples of this doctrine. For instance, under article III, section 1, in our internal taxation we cannot grant special relief to home-produced products by, let us say, a tax concession on Canadian-produced petroleum. We would not be allowed to do that. I am not saying at this moment that we want to do it. I do not think we do it at this moment But will there never be a time when we might want to do that in order to stimulate one of our home industries?
Under paragraph 3 of article III we cannot grant special treatment with respect to the domestic sale, transportation, distribution or use of home-produced goods. I ask the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply what effect that will have on the payment of subventions to bring coal to Ontario from Nova Scotia or Alberta. Again, under paragraph 3 of that same article we cannot raise the Canadian content of goods being manufactured in Canada beyond that which obtains at present. The minister may say we shall never want to do that in future-

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext: What is that again?

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext: We cannot raise the Canadian content of goods manufactured in Canadian factories; we cannot insist that a greater percentage be Canadian, either for consumption in Canada or for export to other countries.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext: We do that every day.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
But we cannot do it under article III, paragraph 3, of this agreement. There is no question but that we are free to do it today. I ask the minister seriously to consider whether we shall be able to do that in future if we accept this agreement.
Then, under article V, of course the restrictions we have imposed upon trucking in bond and so on, are denied us. That may be good or bad, but I want the house to know that is the position.
Then we come to an interesting clause in article XI, which provides that no prohibition or restriction, other than a duty, tax or other charge, may be placed upon the import of goods to Canada or the export of any product from Canada. I have considered the wording of that section very carefully, and I am satisfied that, in terms, it prevents us from placing an embargo upon the export of raw materials in their natural state. When we accept this agreement we shall not be able directly to prohibit the export of pulpwood or logs from British Columbia, for instance, or salmon before it is canned, or anything of that nature. I do not suppose we could directly prohibit the export of iron ore or base metals before they were manufactured. It may be that the minister will say we shall never want to do that. But I thought he made the statement not so long ago that he was going to build up and develop the economy of this country. Certainly, under these clauses his power to do that in any of the usual ways will be vastly curtailed.
I have stated some of the absolute prohibitions. I would not want the house to believe there were not escape clauses from them, and for a moment I want to discuss those escape clauses. The most important escape clause as far as Canada is concerned is article XVIII, which gives power to adopt, for the promotion of economic development, any non-discriminatory protective measure, but with the qualification that the plan must first be submitted to and approved by the international trade organization. I think we should consider that clause very carefully and see whether we want our plans for the building up of Canadian industry or for the development of Canadian mines and forests to be subject to approval of the international trade organization, no

Tariffs and Trade
matter how benevolent the intentions of that organization may be. It is possible that we want to do that; it may be that the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, for instance, will never want to apply any of those practices again. But he is applying them now and he is. going to continue to apply them for quite a few years, so he is going to have to take advantage of these escape clauses. Can he say or can the government say we shall never want to take advantage of these escape clauses after the present monetary crisis is over? Can he say conditions in the world will always be so good that we shall not have to avail ourselves of any of these clauses in connection with our economic development?
Another important escape clause is article XVI, which permits the payment of subsidies, subject to the right of the international trade organization to protest and to negotiate limitations. I think the minister mentioned this clause this afternoon. It may be that the method of subsidizing is the only way we shall ever wish to restrict imports to or exports from Canada. I do not know if that is so; certainly on that point I should like the advice of experts.
Then, under articles XII to XIV, power is given to deviate from the agreement if necessary to preserve our external financial position and balance of payments. Well, Mr. Speaker, these clauses concerning the preservation of our external financial position and the balance of payments must be in use by the government already. It seems to me a bit unfortunate, if we may adopt these discriminatory methods to bring us back to a certain level, that, once we reach that level, we must immediately desist and not carry on farther. I wonder if our principle is not leading us astray when we consider this application of it. I should like also to draw to the attention of the house the fact that the principle of non-discriimination is carried so far that exceptions to it are permitted only subject to the provision that such action does not cause unnecessary damage to the commercial or economic interests of any other contracting party. Surely the principle of non-discrimination is being carried a bit too far there, when we provide that a country like ours, surrounded by other countries under the same crown and in the same financial position, must have regard to the economic and commercial interest of still other countries in working its way out of a difficult situation.
I want to discuss that point farther, but before doing so I should like to say one thing about escape clauses generally. I do not like them. I should like to see an agreement between these nations which did not have all these escape clauses. When Canada accepts
this agreement I do not think she will want to use escape clauses. Already in the attitude of the government over restrictions I think we have seen that they want to adhere closely to the spirit of the agreement. I suggest to the government that it would be much better to limit any codification of world trade practices to the real principles upon which the nations can agree between themsleves without exception. Then you could go on to build up new principles as a result of experience, instead of attempting to codify at once the whole practice of international trade and provide so many escape clauses that the document will bind only those whose conscience binds them. I think Canada would be one of those countries with such a conscience.
There are some very good things in this agreement. Those clauses which standardize regulations in respect of anti-dumping duties, valuation for custom purposes, and regulations made by the customs departments of the various countries are good indeed. And the idea that the tariff shall be the sole regulator of external trade is, I believe, a fine one, although the government is not practising it and will not be able to practise it. It might be that an agreement limited to definite things would make a greater contribution to wider trade in the world than will this attempt at an over-all codification.
After all, as I said in the beginning, this is an agreement between friends. Friends should be able to talk frankly to each other and agree on real things, rather than agree loosely and then wreck the agreement with escape clauses.
So much for that. I raise these points because I believe that the implication of this untried principle of non-discrimination, even in favour of ourselves, upon our whole destiny as a nation, has not yet been put to any test or fully considered. When I first heard of this "non-discrimination'' principle I wondered if it was a sound principle. Certainly it conflicts with past settled policy in Canada, since confederation.
It is not this country which lea the way to economic nationalism, such as this agreement sets out to prevent. It was not this country; rather it was Germany and Italy which started on the road to political and economic nationalism. Yet in this document there is a perfect escape clause for countries like that. At page 58 we find an absolute exception in respect of any steps taken in time of war or other emergency in international relations. A country such as Italy or Germany, or one similarly situated, on the ground that an emergency	has arisen in international
relations, may be completely freed from this
Tariffs and Trade

document. But Canada, which never led the way in that direction, will be bound by its conscience and by these clauses in its own domestic development.
The economic development clauses affect our sovereignty over our domestic affairs. Within the last few days we have had several examples of their effect. Ministers agreed that they knew' in the spring of this year that we needed to take steps to conserve United States exchange. They knew that about seven months ago; and had they taken those steps, our loss of dollars might have been S500 million less. And that $500 million saving would have obviated any need for borrowing from the export-import bank the sum of $300 million.
In the press in the last few days we have read that the United States have been bringing pressure on the Canadian government in respect of its gold subsidy policy. We have seen non-discrimination work hardships on other countries suffering from dollar deficits, too. It is all very well for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to say, as he did last night, that only $5,000,000 worth of trade from Great Britain and $13,000,000 worth of total trade of non-dollar countries has been affected. But the fact is that individual shipments from all these countries have been affected. They have been delayed or cancelled, and they need not have been either delayed or cancelled. Canada could have had the goods represented by those cancelled orders.
I see in the Financial Post the statement that the devaluation of the dollar, which many Canadians think would provide a good answer to some of our difficulties, is not considered favourably by United States authorities, and that is one of the reasons why the Canadian government is not taking what may be a very necessary step. On top of it all, we have these hints and rumours of a bilateral pact with the United States which will get around the Geneva agreement.
