subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks may I say I am glad that even at this late date the government apparently have come to realize the utter futility of depending upon sucli fantastic agreements as the one signed at Bretton Woods to deal with the unbalance of trade with the United States of America and also, incidentally, to deal with the shortage of United States dollars throughout the world. I realize that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) will probably say that was merely one of the things which were going to help with that situation, but I would remind the house that during the discussion on those agreements we were told that they would be the means of meeting the post-war financial needs of the world. In case there is any doubt in anyone's mind about that, I should like to quote a statement made by the Hon. John W. Snyder, secretary of the United States treasury and chairman of the board of governors of the international bank for reconstruction and development and the fund. In his address at the first session of the fund held in 1946, he had this to say:
The fund and the bank were designed to meet both the immediate post-war and longer-term monetary and financial needs of the world.
That statement was made in September, 1946. Then, one year later when the second annual report of the international bank for reconstruction and development was published we find this on page 7:
When the bank's charter was drafted at Bretton Woods in the summer of 1944, high hopes were held that the bank would prove to be the principal instrument for restoring the war-torn nations of the world to economic life. The critical short-range relief needs were -to be met through donations by UNRRA; the external financing needed for the more permanent recovery programs was to be supplied by loans from the bank. Recovery was conceived of primarily in terms of rebuilding of factories, mines, railroads and other specific productive facilities.
We now know that the problem is deeper and more difficult than was envisaged at Bretton Woods.
At the time of the discussion we pointed out that UNRRA could not begin to deal with rehabilitation. In the early stages it might have, but it was amended into a straight relief project. We suggested that mutual aid or lend-lease should be adopted after the war until such time as the war devastated nations had rebuilt their industries and were once more in a position where they could pay for imports with exports. At that time our proposals were called idealistic, but today we have the Marshall plan which is nothing more or less than a system of mutual aid. But it
Tariffs and Trade

is just two years too late. Had that plan been brought down immediately after the war, a great deal of the grief and hatred which have been generated in Europe might have been avoided. Incidentally, the result has been that many nations have been driven into the sphere of the Soviet Union.
Ever since the end of the war, government officials have been emphasizing that a system of multilateral trade and convertibility of currency would help to solve our unbalance of trade with the United States of America. While United States and Canadian monetary experts have been busily engaged in extolling the great benefits of this proposal, the situation throughout the world has been growing steadily worse. It will be remembered that the financial agreement signed last year by the United Kingdom with the United States committing the United Kingdom to a policy of non-discrimination and convertibility of currency, by July of this year precipitated a serious crisis in that country, while in Canada our unbalance of trade with the United States has been steadily increasing.
I find it hard to understand why the government has been so long in moving to correct that situation, instead of blindly depending upon such proposals as the convertibility of currency and multilateral trade to deal with the situation. I recall that when we were discussing the loan to Great Britain, the then Minister of Finance pointed out that we would not be obliged to use the credits we obtained in that country for the purpose of bringing imports into this country, that we would be able to use those credits for the purpose of meeting an unbalance of trade with the United States. When that was stated, we pointed out that the United Kingdom would not be able to convert its currency into United States dollars unless the United States were prepared to buy from the United Kingdom, thereby providing them with dollars for that purpose.
We in this group have emphasized the need for the re-implementation of the Hyde Park agreement in a modified form, and failing an expansion of exports to the United States and a restriction of imports from that country. Otherwise the result must be an increase in debt to the United States, a situation that should not for one moment be tolerated by this house or this country.
The justification I think for the re-implementation of the Hyde Park agreement is that Canada has unquestionably, since the war. made a far greater contribution, on a per capita basis, than the United States. I base that remark.on a statement which appears in

the report of the international bank for reconstruction, where at page 7 it is stated:
Total post-war assistance extended by Canada has been more than $2,050 million. Swedish aid has been the equivalent of about $800 million and the total credits and grants from the United States have aggregated approximately $15,000 million.
Taking the population of Canada at about 12,000,000 and that of the United States at about 140,000,000, the United States contribution should have been well over S20 billion, in order to be on a parity with the contribution made by Canada. [DOT]
The people of Canada are today being told that they are living beyond their means and that they must accept some form of austerity program. I listened to the Minister of Finance as he modified the term "austerity" program; nevertheless that term has been taken up by the newspapers of this country from one end of the dominion to the other.
I would say, in the first place, that there is no truth in the statement that we in this country are living beyond our means. Nor is there any justification for the second statement so long as we follow sane foreign trade practices, apart, of course, from our moral obligation to help the war devastated countries of Europe.
Let us take the first charge that we are living beyond our means. If that charge is true, then unquestionably Canada must be consuming more than she produces and we must have an unfavourable balance of trade with the world at large. But what is the actual situation. Page 12, table 2 of the foreign exchange control board's report for 1946 show's that we had a net favourable balance of payments with the world at large of S450 million, and deducting from that mutual aid and relief we had a net balance of S351 million. So it cannot be argued that v'e are consuming more than we produce. If we take the first nine months of this year we shall find that the balance has been reduced, but in spite of that fact we still have a considerable balance in our favour. So I would say that it is not so much a question of living: beyond our means as that we are buying too much from the United States and not enough from the other countries of the world. Of course that is not a new situation for Canada, nor is it peculiar to Canada alone. It was the situation of many countries throughout the world prior to 1939, with the result that the gold reserves of the various nations of the world were drained away into the United States and we had the great depression of the 1930's.

Tariffs and Trade
Therefore it must be quite evident that a great deal of the chaos which existed between the two world wars was due to the international trade policies of the United States of America because the United States failed to realize and live up to the principle that international trade must be a two-way street. Instead, she demanded, in return for her exports, either gold or United States dollars, instead of being willing to accept the products of other nations.
I realize that this government is a great exponent of multilateral trade and1 the convertibility of currency. On paper both these schemes look fine. So did the old gold standard look fine on paper. But in practice it is absolutely impossible for such policies to work unless the great trading nations of the world are willing to live up to the very purpose of international trade and accept goods and services in payment for their exports. That is the real purpose of international trade -barter for mutual advantage. That is one of the main reasons why the members of this group so bitterly opposed the Bretton Woods agreement, which was supposed to facilitate the balancing of international trade. But it placed the main responsibility for accomplishing that result upon the debtor nations and imposed severe penalties upon those nations which failed to balance their trade. On the other hand, we realize that today there is also a direct responsibility upon the creditor nations for bringing about a balance of trade. Yet in spite of that fact, no pressure or penalties were applied against creditor nations which failed to accept goods in payment of their exports and thereby forced other nations to have an unbalance of trade. When we were discussing that point we were told time and again that the need for pressure upon creditor nations which we were emphasizing would be taken care of later by certain international trade agreements. Now we have the international trade agreements before us. Like other members, I have found it very hard to get a thorough understanding of these agreements in the short time we have' had them before us, .but I have read the agreerrents through several times very carefully, trying to find some single article or section or clause that places any pressure upon the creditor nations to accept goods in payment for their exports. That is what we were told, during the discussion on Bretton Woods, would be done under these international agreements. Yet we find that absolutely no pressure whatsoever is being placed upon these creditor nations to accomplish that result.
I was interested in a statement that appeared in Saturday Night of November 15.
headed "Trend of world trade is still bilateral," by John L. Marston, Saturday Night's financial correspondent in London. He had this to say:
In the long-drawn-out negotiations at Geneva the real stumbling-block was the United States* t reluctance to open up the home market in return for the freeing of overseas markets for United States exports.
So in exactly the same way that they refused to allow pressure to be brought upon creditor nations under the Bretton Woods agreement, they are still taking the stand that these great nations shall have no pressure applied against them to open up their markets and accept imports in payment for exports. He goes on to say:
These agreements do undoubtedly satisfy the Americans to the extent that they allow rather more freedom of trade to U.S. exporters, while not seriously weakening the great protectionist structure behind which U.S. industry is sheltered (to the detriment, as all the world can now see i-n the dollar famine, of U.S. exporters).
But the agreements are not such as to open the way to multilateral trading in the true sense, and it is quite unlikely that they will reverse the trend towards bilateral pacts, on -the barter principle, which have characterized postwar trading.
I think all members will agree that the lowering of tariffs denes not necessarily mean that any nation has any intention of increasing its imports to balance its exports. This situation was also referred to by the deputy minister of trade and commerce in an address to members of the Electrical Manufacturers Association on October 9, as reported in Foreign Trade of October 18, 1947, from which I quote briefly. He had this to say:
But unless some ways can be found by which the United States will buy more of our products, it is difficult to see how we can continue to be such a valuable customer of the United States.
This is a subject that I suggest is worthy of most serious consideration. It is to be hoped that the I.T.O. conference, in Geneva, will result in some real improvement in such barriers as undoubtedly do exist at the present time. I would like -to repeat, how'ever. what I have said on other occasions, that in the difficult years that are immediately ahead of us, it is, more than ever before, our own resourcefulness that is going to count.
And I should like to interject that if we are to depend upon our own resourcefulness it is important that we do not enter into international agreements of this kind that may restrict our ability to develop our resources.
Then, on the last page he has this to say:
Now that the multilateral system of payments has suffered a serious breakdown for the second time, or perhaps one should say for the third -time in the last generation, Canada and all
Tariffs and Trade

other countries that are engaged heavily in international trade are facing a difficult stage in their affairs. The balance of trade between pairs of countries-that is, the bilateral balance -has become a matter of first importance and will remain so until the mechanism of the multilateral system has once more been placed in ' good order.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that until the United States of America prove by their action that they recognize their obligation to accept payment for exports with imports, Canada should refuse to take any action which would limit its ability to execute bilateral trade agreements. Multilateral trade can be achieved only when nations recognize and live up to the principle that international trade is a two-way street. Therefore, having in mind the tragic consequences of previous attempts to bring about convertibility and multilateral trade, I am somewhat surprised that Canada should today propose to place itself in the type of strait-jacket provided for in the final act, thereby greatly restricting our ability to develop our resources for the benefit of our people.
Why have attempts at multilateral trade failed in the past? I would say, because the true purpose of foreign trading has been lost sight of, namely, the exchange of goods and services on a basis of mutual . advantage. Instead, nations have attempted to use international trade for the purpose of maintaining full employment in their own country at the expense of some other nation; in other words, an attempt to export their unemployment problem. Therefore I would say that until nations are definitely committed to the true purpose of international trade, multilateral trade is doomed.
I wish to discuss briefly the policy laid down in the final act with regard to the general elimination of quantitative restrictions and the policy of non-discrimination. I turn, first of all, to article XI, the heading of which is "General elimination of quantitative restrictions." Then, if we turn to article XII we find the following, "Restrictions to safeguard the balance of payments." Quantitative restrictions are allowed where a nation has an unfavourable balance of trade. But when we turn to article XIII we find that a nation with an unbalance of trade can only place restrictions against the imports of one nation, provided that it places similar restrictions against all other nations at the same time. It is true that in article XIV there is an escape clause.
I just wish to read it. It states that the rule of non-discrimination need not apply to nations with an unbalance of trade provided, and this is the point I want to read:
Provided that
(i) levels of delivered prices for products so imported are not established substantially 
higher than those ruling for comparable goods regularly available from other contracting parties, . . .
I understand it is under that clause that today we are prohibiting imports of certain goods from Britain. It might be argued that, under section 6 of this article, we need not follow that section because section 6 states that this need not come into force until 1949. However, I understand it is the intention or the desire of the government to live up to the principle of the agreement and not make use of the escape clause to a greater extent than absolutely necessary. The point that we take great exception to in that type of policy is this. Surely, when a nation has an unfavourable balance of trade with one nation and at the same time has a favourable balance of trade with other nations, in order to protect its unbalance of trade with the first nation it should have the right to place a restriction on the imports from that nation without having to place any restriction on the imports from those nations with which it has a favourable balance of payments.
Take the position of Canada today. We have an unfavourable balance of trade with the United States of America; we have a favourable balance of trade with Europe, and yet under these agreements we are not allowed to place a restriction against imports from the United States of America unless at the same time we place similar restrictions on imports from other countries. When you have an unfavourable balance of trade with one nation and a favourable balance of trade with another, surely the logical thing would be to restrict the imports from that nation with which you have an unfavourable balance of trade and actually increase the imports from the nation with which you have a favourable balance of trade. But that is not permitted under this act. As I said, we are not actually governed by it until 1949; but when we reach March, 1952, if the contracting parties decide that the situation is such that that escape clause is no longer necessary it is wiped out, and then a nation is compelled to place restrictions against all nations, even though it may have an unfavourable balance of trade with only one.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Just before the house rose at six o'clock I had been discussing the policy of so-called non-discrimination under the Geneva agreements, which is, I believe, a policy that might very well become one of

Tariffs and Trade
vicious discrimination against the weaker nations; and I was somewhat surprised at the defence put up by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) regarding this policy. He appeared to rest his case chiefly upon the fact that the United States of America were insisting upon a policy of non-discrimination and that therefore Canada should tag along and play Charlie McCarthy.
Before leaving the agreements, I should like to touch briefly on article XVI and article XX. Article XVI deals with the question of subsidies. Before we leave this matter, I very much hope that a minister of the government will give the government's interpretation of exactly what that will mean to Canada. The article reads as follows:
Article XVI Subsidies
If any contracting party grants or maintains any subsidy, including any form of income or price support, which operates directly or indirectly to increase exports of any product from, or to reduce imports of any product into, its territory, it shall notify the contracting parties in writing of the extent and nature of the subsidization. of the estimated effect of the subsidization on the quantity of the affected product or products imported into or exported from its territory and of the circumstances making the subsidization necessary. In any ease in which it is determined that serious prejudice to the interests of any other contracting party is caused or threatened by any such subsidization, the contracting party granting the subsidy shall, upon request, discuss with the other contracting party or parties concerned, or with the contracting parties, the possibility of limiting the subsidization.
It seems to me that at least in principle that does limit our ability to subsidize agricultural products in this country or to maintain parity prices. If we establish parity prices in this country, and export wheat, at a price well below the parity price, and then one of the contracting parties, say the Argentine, claimed that that was to the detriment of their nation and the contracting parties so decided, then at least in principle we would be under an obligation to reduce the amount of the subsidy on wheat in this country. The same thing would apply to subsidies on any other primary product or, for that matter, on any commodity in this country.
Then let us take article XX. It is headed "General exceptions", and reads as follows:
Subject to the requirement that such measures are not applied in a manner which would constitute a means of arbitrary or unjustifiable discrimination between countries where the same conditions prevail, or a disguised restriction on international trade, nothing in this agreement shall be construed to prevent the adoption or enforcement by any contracting party of measures-
And then I go down to (g):
Relating to the conservation of exhaustible natural resources if such measures are made effective in conjunction with restrictions on domestic production or consumption.
I take it that means that if we have certain resources of an exhaustible character which we are exporting, and decide that we must conserve these resources, then we would not be in a position to reduce the amount of exports of that commodity unless at the same time we reduced the production or consumption of that commodity in this country. Personally I cannot see any justification for allowing outside authorities to dictate our internal policy in such a way, especially when it might be greatly to the detriment of the people of this country.
In closing, I should like to say it seems to me that this measure will still further encourage the federal government's game of passing the buck. In the 1930's we were continually being told that we cannot improve our condition because it is due to an international situation. In the future, no doubt we shall be told that we cannot do this or we cannot do that because it is contrary to the regulations under the international trade organization, the Bretton Woods agreement or some other form of agreement that we have signed. It seems to me that this, along with some of the other measures that have been passed in recent sessions, is just another attempt to introduce world dictatorship through the back door and reduce this nation to a state of impotency. Fortunately, I do not believe that this house will be so easily hoodwinked on this measure as they were on the Bretton Woods agreement. For that reason I was glad to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) say that this measure would be referred to a committee of the house and that every opportunity would be given for a full investigation into it.
Mr. GORDON B. ISNOR (Halifax): I wish to take part very briefly, Mr. Speaker, in this discussion dealing particularly with the Geneva trade agreement as we understand it. I want to say a few words because of the effect it will have on the eastern section of our country from which I come, particularly with relation to the maritime provinces. In connection with the negotiation of the trade agreement, may I first say how pleased I was that the deputy minister of fisheries, Mr. Stewart Bates, attended at the trade conference. I think in a measure we can thank him for the representations made on behalf of the fishing industry, and for some of the features of this trade agreement. I was somewhat surprised this afternoon at the attitude adopted by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt)
Tariffs and Trade

in making his approach in a rather political manner and accusing the Prime Minister of this country (Mr. Mackenzie King) of placing this big and important question before us in a political sense and giving it a political background. Coming as the hon. member does from British Columbia, I would have thought that he would be particularly pleased with the terms of this agreement, with one possible exception, namely, canned salmon.

Just a minute-from British Columbia and other sections sitting to the left of the Speaker. I had that in mind when I just made brief reference to the attitude of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. Surely he does not overlook the fact that, in the 1911 election, his party created and carried throughout Canada the cry, "No truck or trade with the Yankees." It was unfortunate, I say, that the reciprocity agreement was not brought into effect in 1911, as far as we in the maritimes and particularly those of us in Nova Scotia are concerned. I say with regret that perhaps we would have been in' a far better position than we are today if that had been done. But the fact that the country made that mistake is no reason why we should not continue the practice adopted in later years and make trade agreements which will benefit the country.
I do not want to go back over the imperial preferences, which date back some fifty years, having been created in 1898, revised in 1932, and enlarged in a more beneficial manner in 1937. I want to deal with this agreement as it affects my section of the country. We are particularly interested in two items; that is, fish and lumber. Lumber is among those items on which new and greater concessions have been given. The imposts on sawn and dressed boards of fir, hemlock, larch pine and spruce

have been reduced from $2 to $1 per thousand board feet, a reduction of fifty per cent. The duty free entry of other species of soft wood is bound, so we have no loss there. There is also a reduction in the tariff on cedar to seventy-five cents per thousand board feet, and certain hardwoods enter duty free. Others are bound at 81.50 per thousand board feet. This gives us an enlarged natural market for the lumber of the maritimes. In 1946 Canadian lumber exports to the United States were valued at $59,199,000, a sizeable business in itself.

May I offer a further word to my fishermen friends of the maritime provinces, particularly? The fishing industry will benefit from the United States concessions on nearly all species of processed fish. Certain branches of the industry which, in the spring of 1947, were faced with a sharp drop in demand will now have greater access to the United States market.
The duty on fresh or frozen salmon and halibut has been cut from one cent to one-half cent a pound. The rates on fresh mackerel, formerly at one cent a pound, and on frozen mackerel formerly at li cents, have both been reduced to j cent a pound. On fresh or frozen fillets of cod, haddock, hake, pollock the rate has been bound as at present.
There also have been reductions on many textile products of which Canada is a large importer. If I remember correctly, there are something like 600 items listed in the most-favoured-nations schedule. Some of the Canadian reductions will not immediately affect importations, as was mentioned a minute ago; but I do feel that, taking the long view of this agreement, we in the maritime provinces will certainly benefit to a very great extent.
There is one observation I should like to express to the government, and I hope Your Honour will not call me to order if I interject a thought respecting the shipment of goods through Canadian ports. I was pleased the other day when my colleague from Halifax (Mr. Dickey) spoke as he did with respect to

a greater use being made of our Canadian ports. I should like to compliment him upon his excellent presentation at that time, and upon the able manner in which he placed his case before the house. It was an indication of the fine type of man we have, when we see this young man in the house as a representative from my constituency. I am sure all who listened to him were much impressed, and I feel that, as the years go by, the people of Halifax will be proud to have him as their representative in the House of Commons.
I wanted to say a word or two about shipping through Canadian ports. I think shippers in.all parts of Canada should make every possible use of Canadian ports, and I have more particularly in mind those fine ports on the Atlantic. I believe all hon. members know what a wonderful harbour there is at Halifax and I need hardly mention it. I have spoken of it quite often, and the port received considerable advertising during the war because of its fine performance. I sincerely trust that, when I again bring this matter to the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) and others, they will not overlook the possibilities of using this port to the fullest extent.
I close by again expressing the thought which, I feel, is uppermost in the minds of maritimers, that these agreements will expand our trade and be of real benefit to the people of those provinces.

GREEN (Vancouver South): Mr. Speaker, I know that you and eveiy hon. member of this house will bear with me for a few moments before I begin to discuss the resolution before us, while I say a word in appreciation of the Hon. Tarifjs and Trade
I urge the government to call a by-election in Yale just as soon as possible so that the riding may be represented here when we reconvene after the New Year. I make that request because the riding of Yale is . vitally interested in these trade treaties. I doubt if there is another riding in Canada w-hich is so directly concerned with the treaties now under consideration by this house. The riding is made up of the Okanagan valley which runs for many miles north and south between two mountain ranges. Off to the southeast there is another fertile area known as the Boundary country, and to the southwest another known as the Princeton area.
In this riding there are important mining and lumbering industries, but the main one is the growing of fruit. Not so many years ago men and women came into that portion of our province and, by their energy and foresight, brought the waters from the mountains out onto the dry bench lands and thus developed a remarkably fertile area. Not only did they develop ranches for the growing of fruit, but over the years they have gradually built up a splendid processing industry for the making of fruit juices and various by-products of fruit. I do not believe that there are three finer or more progressive small cities in Canada than the cities of ''Vernon, Kelowna and Penticton which lie in the Okanagan valley.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext: And Chilliwack.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Because of my friendship for the hon. member for Fraser Valley, (Mr. Cruickshank) I will put the city of Chilliwack in the same class. The principal fruit grown in the area is the apple. When you think of apples anywhere in Canada you think of the Okanagan. When members from the fruit ridings of Ontario or the fruit ridings of Nova Scotia want to buy an apple here in Ottawa even they ask for and always get Okanagan apples.
This development has been achieved only through a long and hard struggle. There has always been the stiffest competition between the Canadian Okanagan valley and the Washington state Okanagan valley, which is really a continuation of the same valley. There is a larger area under cultivation in the state of Washington; their fruit ripens a bit earlier, and they have a much larger home market than the Canadian Okanagan valley. The result has been stiff competition from the state of Washington as well as from the state of Oregon.
British Columbia apples have been dealt a very severe blow by these Geneva treaties. I do not believe there is an hon. member from British Columbia who will deny that fact, no
matter what party he represents. I submit that the people of Yale have been sacrificed by this trade treaty, primarily because they have lost their preference in the United Kingdom market. I would refer hon. members to a press release which was issued by the government to explain the treaties. On page 11 we find an explanation of just what has happened to apples, and I quote:
One of Canada's most important contributions to the general agreement on tariffs and^ trade which has for its purpose the reduction of tariffs, the elimination of tariff preferences and other trade restrictions is the relinquishing of the apple preference in the United Kingdom.
The apple preference in the United Kingdom is gone. The press release goes on to explain that Canadian apples have always enjoyed free entry to the United Kingdom, but that by virtue of the Ottawa agreements a tariff was placed against apples from other parts of the world. So far as British Columbia was concerned, the important factor was that tariffs were placed against apples from the states of Washington and Oregon.
The press release goes on to say:
At Geneva Canada agreed to the elimination of the apple preference during the northern hemisphere marketing season so that now apples from all sources enter the United Kingdom market free of duty from August 16 to April 15 inclusive.
That is the important period. The apple growers have been called on to make more than their fair share of the contributions necessary to make these treaties possible. The compensation that is given is also listed in this press release. Here it is:
Compensation for the apple concession is obtained mainly from the United States hut it cannot be matched with any single item among the United States concessions. It is a part of a mutually advantageous agreement between Canada and its neighbour and other contracting parties.
What has happened in effect as between Canada and the United States is that there has been a small reduction of the Canadian duty against United States apples and a small reduction of the United States duty against Canadian apples. But in normal times it is impossible for Canada to market her apples in the United States. The United States has made a reduction of 16-66 per cent and Canada has reduced her tariff by 37-5 per cent. The result may very well be that the Okanagan apple growers will also lose their market on the Canadian prairies. Time and again they have had great difficulty in holding that market against the United States, and these changes may make it impossible once again for them to do so. The situation is very
Tariffs and Trade

well summed up in a press dispatch of November 18 from Kelowna, reading as follows:
Elimination of the British preference market will mean a return to the old "cutthroat competition'' between fruit producers for markets, A. K. Lloyd, president and general manager of British Columbia Tree Fruits, said here in commenting on the new trade agreements.
Mr. Lloyd, as the British Columbia members know, is the outstanding figure in the fruit industry in British Columbia. The article goes on to say:
Growers who produced nearly 7,000,000 boxes of apples this year fear that Canadian apples and other fruit will have to compete with U.S. produce for the British market under new agreements.
However growers are also worried that they may lose the prairie market to U.S. fruit which ripens earlier than that grown in the Okanagan.
In addition to apples, other fruits grown in that valley and in other parts of British Columbia, including the Fraser valley, will, I think, suffer from these trade agreements. And so I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that when this matter is discussed in the new year there should be a member sitting in this house speaking for the riding of Yale, and once again I ask the government to call that by-election in time to have a member here when the house sits again.
I have dealt only with apples. There is also something to be said about lumber. Lumber is the main industry in British Columbia. Under the Geneva treaties, lumber has lost half of its preference in the British market. At the same time it has been given wider entry to the United States market. No one can yet tell what the result will be, whether it will be of benefit or whether there will be a loss.
Another important product in my province is canned salmon. Canned salmon has also lost half the preference it had in the United Kingdom market, and on that commodity there lias been no compensation given to the fishing industry. If members will refer to page 20 of the press release they will find the reason why, in these words:
This does not-	.
Referring to canned salmon.
This does not, 'however, apply to canned salmon, of which the United States ordinarily has a large exportable surplus, where the duty is bound at the existing rate of 25 per cent ad valorem.
In other words, the United States have refused to give any concession on canned salmon because they have an exportable surplus themselves. What has happened is this, and I am sure that the hon. member for New

Westminster (Mr. Reid) will agree with me because he is an expert on commercial fishing-

speechtext: There are other reasons for the twenty-five per cent ad valorem.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Here is what has been done. The United States duty on fresh salmon has been cut from one cent to half a cent a pound. Fresh salmon are already being bought by United States canners. The price is higher in the United States than in Canada, and it will be that much easier for the fresh salmon to get into the United States market once these treaties go through. The United States buyer is buying our salmon to process them, and the result will be that the Canadian canneries will be unable to get fresh salmon. That will affect the livelihood of at least 10,000 people who are working in our canneries. The result may very well be that Canadian canning companies will be forced to go across the boundary and set up canneries in the United States in order to can Canadian fish, and young Canadians will probably have to follow them across the boundary to get work. There has been a very strong protest made to this government by the minister of fisheries of British Columbia. I have here a press dispatch containing his protest. He points out the various factors to which I have referred and says, for example :
Action which has the effect of shipping raw material out of the province which can be manufactured or processed here is a most retrogressive step.
The cuts in the British preference so far as British Columbia is concerned are serious. But what remains of the British preference is of great value to us. The preference that remains on lumber is of great value and also the preference that remains on canned salmon. Under these Geneva treaties, these preferences which remain need not be touched. Provision is made in the Geneva treaties that the preference agreements may continue in effect.. Take, for example, what is called the Canada-United Kingdom trade agreement. That'.can continue in effect, also, the agreement with Australia and the ones with New Zealand, South Africa and Rhodesia. All these continue in effect, but of course they contain a six months' termination clause. If either country wishes to terminate the agreement all that needs to be done is for it to give six months' notice, and that is quite permissible under these new Geneva treaties.
But the sad fact is. Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie

Tariffs and Trade
King) has gone much farther. He has demanded and he has obtained from the British government the right to reduce or eliminate the British preference; to reduce or eliminate the British preference overnight. That will be found in the exchange of notes appearing on page 100 of the final act which the members have in their hands. In the letter from Canada to the United Kingdom of October 30, 1947, we find this provision telling them what they have to agree to:
The government of the United Kingdom recognize the right of the government of Canada 'to reduce or eliminate such preferences.
Meaning what remains of the British preference. That has this effect: if the government wishes to negotiate again with the United States covering some commodity on which we still have a preference, then that particular commodity can be taken out of the British preference; over-night one commodity can be taken out; next month another commodity can be taken out, or they can be all taken out- without the formality of giving any notice whatsoever. That means there is no stability remaining in connection with the trade covered by these preferences. It may very well mean that the preferences are ruined.
It is interesting to read the reply- from the British government to this long letter written by Canada. It consists of just four lines, showing that they had been put on the spot. Here is what it says on page 106:
Sir,
In acknowledging receipt of your letter of today's date in regard to the 1937 trade agreement between the United Kingdom and Canada, I wish on behalf of His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom to express their agreement with what is stated therein.
That is addressed to the chairman of the Canadian delegation at Geneva. In the press release we find the government boasting of what has happened. I refer hon. members to page 4 where we find these words:
There has been concluded on Canada's initiative-
If you please.

a revision of the Canada-United Kingdom trade agreement, 1937. The exchange of letters in this regard is being made public with this announcement. Under this exchange of letters each country undertakes, with respect to goods covered by the relevant schedules of the multilateral agreement to continue to accord to the products of the other treatment no less favourable in general than has been accorded under the existing agreement of 1937, but in^ which also each government recognizes the right of the other to reduce or eliminate preferences. In taking such initiative the Canadian government has had in mind the histori i Canadian
attitude respecting preferences, namely, that these concessions, freely given, are not matters of rigid contractual right or obligation.
That is stating what has happened with regard to the United Kingdom. But we also find this:
It is the intention of the Canadian government to propose to the other commonwealth governments concerned agreements with them similar to that now concluded between this country and the United Kingdom.
In other words, the Canadian Prime Minister is now going to go to Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and to the other empire nations with which we have agreements and say the very same thing to them, that Canada insists on having the right to cancel these preferences or change them over-night. That is why we moved the motion we did this afternoon. We think this policy of the government is wrong; we do not think it can be justified. We think it is very much against the best interests of Canada, and once we get the procedure straightened out, I propose to move the following amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol).

If Canada is to play its part in furthering the objectives of the international trade organization, it is important that the Canadian government should have freedom to detei mine the

This is a policy of isolation within the commonwealth and, Mr. Speaker, that is a very dangerous attitude for a partner to adopt in any partnership, no matter whether it is a partnership of nations or partners in a commercial business or in a profession. It is a very dangerous attitude for a partner to adopt, and it is a very dangerous attitude for Canada that has been taken by our Prime Minister.

speechtext: So much for the preferences. Now I go on to a further point, Mr. Speaker. The purpose of these Geneva treaties, so we are told, is to free trade, to make for freer trade across the world. That was the lovely, rosy picture the Prime Minister painted here last night. If he believes that-if he really does believe something this time-there is a move he can make at once and it is this. He can lift the prohibition on imports into Canada from commonwealth nations and from countries to which we have lent money. We demand that that be done at this session. Here, under this austerity program, we actually have an embargo placed on importations from those empire countries and from the very countries to whom we have lent hundreds of millions of dollars, and that embargo is placed on their imports because we have been buying too much from the United States.

speechtext: That is Liberal logic.

That is some more of this wonderful Liberal trade policy. Canadians need these goods. Britain, Australia and other nations of the commonwealth, as well as France, the Netherlands and Belgium want to be able to send us goods in order to pay off the loans that we have made to them. Let us consider Australia; and we on the Pacific coast are vitally interested in Australia. Certain imports from Australia were cut off over-night. I have here a press dispatch of November 26 from Canberra which reads as follows:
Prime Minister Chifley has told the parliamentary Labour Party that Australia's dollar position is deteriorating daily and further severe import restrictions from dollar areas will have to be imposed soon, Reuters News Agency said todav.
The report came as Canada's import ban on Australian canned fruits shocked Queensland pineapple growers. The growers said first news of the embargo, caused by Canada's own import restriction policy imposed last week, was cancellation of a Canadian order for 3,006 cases of canned pineapples packed from the winter crop.
Our trade with Australia is one-sided as it is. I have here the figures for each of the years from 1941 to 1946 inclusive and for the nine months ended September, 1947. Our imports from Australia in those years were S104 million odd. Our exports were almost three times as great, namely, $321 million odd. The balance of trade against Australia was $217 million odd. And now the Canadian
government just arbitrarily shuts off these imports from Australia. That is shabby treatment of a sister nation, Mr. Speaker, and the prohibition of imports is shabby and foolish treatment of our allies who want to repay us the money they have borrowed from us. The ridiculous part of it all is that such a procedure was not necessary under these Geneva treaties. Provision is actually made under article XIV, paragraph 6, clause (a), whereby Canada did not need to take that course at all. Yet it has been done. Last night the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) gave the answer, this Minister of Finance who takes all these things so light-heartedly, although out across the country he has made hundreds of Canadians face ruin by his actions in the last few weeks, and by his delay of months in taking steps to meet this emergency situation. He gave the reason last night and it will be found on page 95 of Hansard. The reason is this:
The United States in particular attaches great importance to the non-discrimination principle. While it possibly could not be called a fetish with them, it is a principle to which great importance is attached. The success of this emergency program and the smooth functioning of our economy depend upon the whole-hearted cooperation of our friends to the south. Today, instead of a drive
to develop Canada, we find a drift into dependence on the United States, with this Mackenzie King government leading the way. The Prime Minister spoke of the wonderful timing he had given this austerity program. Actually the timing was this: the government was waiting for the Marshall plan, leaning on the United States, hoping the United States

would come along and drag us out of our troubles. One result is that Canada now has to go to the United States on bended knee and ask for a loan, which never would have been necessary if this government had moved to meet the situation earlier. I may tell the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that this American loan is not popular in British Columbia with the people of any party, even among his own followers.
This drift into dependence upon the United States is admitted here in Canada; it is being talked about in the press. I have here an editorial from the Vancouver Sun of November 25 and the Sun is a supporter of this government.

The minister has had a good deal of help from it. The Sun said:
The great plan

of which Mr. Howe is to be principal designer-to re-orient Canadian industry fits neatly into this Washington picture. That plan, as presently understood by the Canadian man in the street, is intended to reduce Canada's dependence upon American-made goods, and at the same time increase Canadian sales to the United States. As it is understood in those Washington circles which have bothered to think about it-
This is the point I emphasize:
[DOT]-it means that Canadian production would be tailored to supplement that of the United States.
A week ago Suhday we had Walter Winched, the famous American radio commentator, saying something to this effect:	"At a
very early date Canada and the United States are entering into an economic union." Then there is this foreign letter from the Whaley-Eaton Service, a reliable Washington service, which was read this afternoon by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt) but part of which I should like to repeat:
Also, in consequence, Canada would tailor her whole production in such manner as to supplement-
To supplement, if you please!
-that of the U.S.; as far as could be achieved without damage to the immediate needs of Europe's recovery, she would concentrate her agriculture, mining and industry on the chinks in America's productive armour.
If this drift continues there can be only one end: Canada will be a satellite of the United States, and that is a very dim future for this nation. We must not sponge on the United States economically or for our ideas or for our defence. Mind, you, Mr. Speaker, the temptation to do so is perfectly natural. It has always been there and always will be. Ours is a far-flung nation, with the people settled in a narrow strip along the boundary,

Tariffs and Trade
living beside a much stronger nation of many more people. The temptation will always be there. It is here now; the temptation is great now, because the United States is the greatest power in the world. Mind you, that country could not be more friendly to us than it is at the present time, and for the United States we have the most friendly feelings in return. That nation is now leading the world. It did not ask for the position but had it thrust upon it by virtue of the war, and is accepting the responsibility in a splendid way. So I say that today there is a tremendous temptation for Canada to lean on the United States. And there will be that temptation in future.
But from the very beginning of this nation, right from the time when there were no English-speaking people in Canada at all, that temptation has been resisted. It was resisted by the ancestors of our French-speaking compatriots hundreds of years ago. They had the same temptation and stood out against it. At various times in the history of Caanda we have stood out against that temptation.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the destiny of Canada is not to be a satellite of the United States but to be a great world power standing beside the other nations of the commonwealth and beside our trusted ally, the United States. If Canada makes that her aim it will be in the best interests, not only of ourselves, but also of the United States They want a strong Canada, standing on her own feet. They want a strong commonwealth able to stand beside them to meet the terrible problems facing the world at the present time.
This is one of those vital times that come every so often in the life of a nation, one of those periods that affect the trend in that nation for decades and perhaps for generations. I urge upon all the members of this house and upon Canadians from coast to coast: let us stop this drift to dependence upon the United States. Instead, let us go all out to develop Canada, our own nation.
Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol):
That the said resolution be not now proceeded with, but that the same be referred to the committee of the whole house with instructions to divide the subject matter thereof into two resolutions, one relating to
"the general agreement on tariffs and trade, including the protocol of provisional application thereof, annexed to the final act of the second session of the preparatory committee of the united nations conference on trade and employment held at Geneva from April 10 to October 30, 1947, together with the complementary agreements of October 30, 1947, between Canada and the United States of America,"
and the other resolution relating to "the complementary agreement of the same date (April 30, 1947), between Canada and the United Kingdom."
Right Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Pensions and National Health): Mr. Speaker, I wish to take only a moment of the time of the house, and I do not wish to be controversial in the slightest degree. In case I wish to take part in this debate later on,
I may have to ask the house for the privilege of doing so, but at the moment I wish to identify myself in the closest and warmest personal way with the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) concerning a gentleman who has left our ranks within these halls, whom I regarded as one of the finest parliamentarians I ever met. In a word, as one who was politically opposed to him, I want to say I never heard this gentleman say an unkind word against a political opponent. He was one of nature's grandest gentlemen. His departure is a great loss to this assembly. Let us hope that he may yet spend many years with his gracious wife and that it may be long before those of us who remain within these halls, may say of him:
This be the verse you grave for me;
Here he lies where he longed to be;
Home is the sailor, home from sea,

Mr. Speaker, I do not join those who have greeted this general agreement on tariffs and trade with eulogies. On the other hand, neither do I join in the condemnation which has been heaped upon it in some quarters. I prefer to reserve judgment. I should like to see this measure submitted to a committee of the house, perhaps the banking and commerce committee, where we can, with the aid of witnesses and preferably those who had some hand in formulating these policies, ascertain the facts and make up our minds with respect jo them. I have formed certain tentative conclusions at the moment, but I am withholding judgment as to whether they are right or wrong. I fear, however, that this general agreement is now only an admirable historical document.
The nations who have signed the general agreement- hope to see the rebuilding of multilateral trade. The success of multilateral trade depends upon the free convertibility of currency. I suggest that there will be very few freely convertible currencies in the world in the predictable future; and, if such is the case, multilateral trade is going to fall by the wayside.
1,58
Tariffs and Trade

I say that if we do not have free convertibility of exchange we shall have no multilateral trade and, regrettably, this agreement will die a-borning. Twenty-three nations have signed it, and I believe that of those 23 only one has what we would call free convertibility of currency. I refer to the United States. We do not in Canada; and we cannot at this juncture afford to have controls raised from our exchange. Anybody who suggests that Canada should return to free exchange is guilty of economic lunacy, because the effect on the workers and farmers of this country would be little short of devastating.
We are faced with the fact that throughout the years we have had an unbalance with the United States. In the past we have made it up by converting currency from other nations into United States dollars. If currencies are frozen we cannot do that. How then do we meet this unbalance with the United States? Since confederation we have imported roughly $27 billion worth of goods and we have exported about $18 billion worth. As I say, this unbalance is perennial. We may try to balance our trade with the United States by increasing exports and by reducing imports, but I do not think either of these measures will solve the problem.
Therefore we are faced with this distinct possibility, that for our economic preservation Canada will be forced into a bilateral agreement with the United States; and when we do that we shoot galley-west the principles which underlie the general agreement on tariff and trade.
I point out these facts for the consideration of the house. I think there is great validity in my fears. Unfortunately, if I a.m right, I am forced to this pessimistic conclusion that this general agreement is not an ignoble memorial of days which are dead and gone.
