speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me say I am very much surprised to hear some of the views which have been expressed in the house recently regarding the liquidation of the British empire in the matter of preferential trade within that empire. After all is said and done, those of us who come from Ontario, including Mr. Deputy Speaker who now occupies the Chair, know that is so.
Let me point out that during the last session of parliament, as far back as February 10, I saw this disaster coming, in view of the fact that the house had passed, almost unanimously, the Bretton Woods agreement, and the further fact that we had accepted the principle of the American loan which, by sections 6, 7 and 8, eliminated any hope of

preferential trade treatment, inasmuch as agreement was given in that loan not to have any discrimination or trade barriers against the United States.
Let us look at this thing from a common-sense point of view-and there is very little common sense shown in the house on some occasions. The people back in the constituencies know more than we do about preferential trade. You, Mr. Deputy Speaker, will know that about 2,500 American industries had to cross the border, under preferential trade, in order to locate their Canadian plants. They established plants and we saw the amount of labour that that produced for Canada.
We in Ontario have supported the principle of preferential trade. Speaking to a meeting in my constituency the other day, I said:
Preferential trade which had saved Canada from an even more severe depression between two wars had received no support other than lip service from any party at Ottawa.
Here we have a proposal with regard to the Geneva agreements. They selected a great place when they chose Geneva for their conference. We spent six or seven millions of dollars of this country's money on trips of members to Geneva. It was supposed to be known as "the booby prize" for those government members appointed by the government for a nice, soft trip there to its sham meetings. The place is ruined today. One can read only two or three lines in the London Times with regard to the closing of the whole sham thing. But they selected a very favourable place for their work on the international trade talks last February.
As I say, we have had nothing but lip service for preferential trade. The government sent its representatives to Geneva who have refused to ask for empire preferences. Away back last spring, the British government asked for an empire conference. With whom was it to be? It was to be with the senior dominions before the Geneva meetings of Canada, Australia and New Zealand, and was to deal with preferential trade. New Zealand and Australia supported the calling of that conference. Where was Canada? She was nowhere; she would not go or attend it. However, as I say, the American loan and the Bretton Woods agreement were agencies in the liquidation and scuttling of the British empire.
In my opinion, terms of the loan from the United States were more like the ruthless and vindictive demands of a victor over a fallen and vanquished foe than an agreement between allies, and it was apparent that but for Britain and the dominions holding out as they did, all would have ended and there would have been a complete collapse of civilization.

Tariffs and Trade
When I addressed the meeting to which I have referred I said:
Geneva crucified any hope of bringing preferential trade up to date and, like John Brown's body, they hanged it on a sour apple tree. Widespread unemployment in Canada would be an indirect consequence of the Bretton-Woods agreement and the American loan tied to it, with the Geneva agreements.
That is correct. There is very little difference if you look at this problem from the beginning, very little difference between it and the reciprocity which was proposed away back in 1924. I spoke in the House of Commons at that time.
I would ask particularly the attention of hon. members from the Toronto district, because we know the value of preferential trade. In the Parkdale riding, and in other Toronto ridings, United States firms, because of the British preference, established plants. I refer particularly to those established in ward 6. Here is what I said back in 1924; and when I said it I was supported by a powerful newspaper, the Toronto Evening Telegram, the only paper I know of which stood up and, as a great British pioneer, supported this principle from the beginning. There may have been one or two others, but I do not know of them.
Speaking in the house in 1924, I said:
All I can say is this that if such a policy of free trade and reciprocity is adopted by the people of the country it means that we will go back to where we were in 1878. Industries will be ruined; people will be out of work and the times will be ten times worse than they are now. I may say further to the Canadian Council of Agriculture that free trade and reciprocity with the United States would make a Lazarus out of a country that Sir Wilfrid Laurier professed to have made a nation. That proposal would exhibit the Canada of Queenston Heights, of St. Julian, of Vimy Ridge, of Passchendaele, of Aimiens and many other fields of glory, as a beggar for the poor favour of reciprocity and free trade.
That is correct. How did this belated proposal come to the house? Why do we have this proposal from the government of the day. who signed it, and is it in effect now? This matter should have been referred to the Supreme Court of Canada on a reference, which has the power to decide such things, as to whether it is legal. The matter came up in the house on February 10 last. The leader of the government, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) replied to a question which I asked on February 10 in connection with empire preference by saying that the government would look into it. I had said to him in the house that the Hon. Doctor Coombs, director general of reconstruction of Australia, had said that "the
empire preference was doomed," no matter how much Australia or other food producing countries wanted to keep it. I asked if the government were prepared to make a statement and the minister said he could not make one then.
There was a meeting in London on March 11. Then the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) moved for the production of certain papers, but they were not brought down, only a copy of a speech by Mr. Attlee in the House of Commons at London, evading it and saying by the American loan clauses 7 to 9 it was out.
This matter may be referred to the committee of the whole house, and all that that committee can do on it now is to conduct a post-mortem. The agreement has been made, signed, sealed and delivered over our heads by the government. The trouble is that we have surrendered all along too much political, financial, economic, military and social power initiative to Washington. That has been the trouble all along. If this agreement goes to a senate committee all they can do is just conduct on it a post-mortem. The United States would respect us much more if we were to tell them the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. All along Great Britain and the British fleet have protected these shores. They have protected them for a hundred years and have given them the best security during four wars, for two centuries. Allowance should be made for that.
This is just playing Santa Claus to America, for Christmas which is two weeks away tomorrow. Some people say, "There ain't no Santa Claus," and a lot of people back home are saying. "There ain't no House of Commons." All these things are being conducted over our heads without any authority. What about the freedom and supremacy of parliament and all that? I have always been a supporter of the British empire. If we take the resources of the motherland and the other countries of the empire it will be found that they are vastly superior to the total resources of either the United States or Russia.
In my opinion, we are going back to the days of the Family Compact in 1837 when the executive ruled the country under crown authority. We have to go back to those days to find anything like what is being proposed here now. The government is going over the head of the law courts and the House of Commons in all this.
I notice that there is a difference between the notice of motion in yesterday's order paper and the one appearing today. The one under date of Wednesday, December 10, is
Tariffs and Trade

at least ten lines shorter than the one that appeared yesterday. The Prime Minister yesterday read the resolution:
Resolved that it is expedient that parliament do approve the general agreement on tariffs and trade

In the motion today, the word "expedient" does not appear. This thing is not expedient, and yet it is going to create widespread unemployment in this country and cause the closing up of a great many industries. It is just free trade and unrestricted reciprocity with the United States. It will mean the ruination of all business, large and small.
On May 9, 1947, I raised this question in the house when reference had been made to preferential duties in the budget. I reasserted the policy of Sir John A. Macdonald who had said back in 1844 that the prosperity of Canada depended upon its permanent connection with the mother country. In 1878 he introduced the policy of protection which made this country great. That is the policy we should follow, the empire first, last and all the time.
Trade, should follow the flag and the flag the trade. We should not give up British preferences. My hon. friends opposite and my hon. friends to the left used to believe in free trade. They said that the grain trade should flow north and south instead of east and west to Britain and our allies, and the result was that on one occasion wheat went down to thirty-eight cents a bushel. Mr. P'ielding and Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1897 brought in preferential trade within the empire and the six cents preference on grain. That policy should have been continued, but it was ended in 1938.
The budget of last May forgot that. I was the only one on these benches who voted against the Bretton Woods agreements. I have always been a strong supporter of preferential trade within the empire and shall *continue to be. I believe that a large body of public opinion supports it at the present time. What did free trade ever do for the [DOT]dominions or for the people of this country? As a result of British preferential trade, 2,500 United States branch plants and affiliated industries were established in this country, many of them being manufacturing establishments. These branch plants were set up in [DOT]Canada to take advantage of the British preference. I will oppose any change in that policy.
In 1945 when Germany was beaten-the mother country with the help of the dominions ' which went it alone for two years was mainly .responsible for the victory-the mother

country was at the height of its power. The same was true of the dominions. Before the announcement was made on November 17 last, we had agreements in force in connection with preferential trade with Great Britain, Eire, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and the British West Indies, as well as with the United States and twenty-eight other countries.
The government has no mandate from the people of Canada for all these leap in the dark agreements. We have tossed empire preferential trade to the four winds just at a time when business, both retail and wholesale, is hamstrung. We launch all this wave of internationalism and totalitarianism without any mandate from the people. No one, not even the Canadian government, knows where it all will lead to. The people, like parliament, are all in the dark with all this maelstrom of countless agreements and petty meddling with trade and commerce. Business has not been consulted and no one knows, where all this will lead to. Our main mistake has been the surrendering of too much financial, military, economic and social initiative to Washington.
Australia, New Zealand and the other dominions held a meeting before the Geneva meeting. Canada refused to attend it. However, we now have these series of agreements which are nothing more than a Chinese puzzle. The empire has been sold down the river. All we have in return is a Marshall plan which, after a year, is still in the blueprint stage. Even the right of Canadians to call themselves British subjects has been cancelled by the Ottawa folly of separatism, isolation and drifting out of the empire.
We are to have a standing army of bureaucrats with autocratic powers. We are losing every semblance of liberty in Canada. For two years the government's economic policy has been made up of controls, rationing, restrictions, priorities, exhortation and inflation. Now that it has landed the country m such a mess, all the government can think of to do is to prescribe a lot more of the same medicine. There are to be new controls over capital investment, and all trade and commerce and imports, the one sure long-term remedy. There are to be tighter allocations of materials.
I received a letter from the founder and author of this policy of the Ottawa agreements of 1932 shortly before he died, from our great Prime Minister, Lord Bennett.
In a letter to me Lord Bennett said:
The only great agricultural market left in the world is Great Britain. We acquired a preference in that market for wheat at six cents a bushel, which Sir Wilfrid Laurier said he

Tariffs and Trade
would give almost anything to secure. It is equally true that the preference on apples and pears, et cetera, meant the sale of 1,000,000 barrels from Nova Scotia in one year. What we lack is markets for our exports, and if anyone thinks that we are going to find in the United States a market or either agricultural products on any substantial scale, or for manufactured goods, I think he will be mistaken ami find that the only thing they are willing to take from us is raw material from which to manufacture finished products.
There is one thing that you must be proud of and that is that you have consistently during a long term of public life realized the value of British markets to Canada, and I am satisfied that on analysis it will be found that there is not much to be obtained by us in foreign countries as markets except for small quantities of our products, and then only when they cannot be secured more cheaply and near at hand.
Keep up your courage. You will not surrender the convictions you have held so well during a fairly long lifetime. I really find it difficult to think that Canadians do not realize that except for agricultural products we have no substantial markets except those of the United Kingdom. We will hope for the best.
In his last speech in the House of Lords just ten days before he died, Lord Bennett made a prophecy when he saw what was being done then. He said that, in the days to come, history would say that the abandonment of the British preference was the empire's darkest hour.
The government of the day has no mandate from the people of this country to put through these agreements. I have a great admiration for the United States. I admire what they have done. They deserve great credit for lease-lend and for their plan to aid Europe, but I regret that for two and a half years Britain, with the aid of the dominions, fought the last war alone. The United States today is going back to the days of the economic power politics.
This policy is short-sighted and wholly mistaken from the point of view of the United States' own interests. If successful, it can lead only to a repetition of the disaster of 1931, from which the United States suffered more than the rest of the world. Any loans which the United States grants to Europe on its terms cannot possibly be repaid, while the loans will, sooner or later, be universally repudiated. Mr. Amery said that the fatal mistake made by Great Britain and, in large measure, by other countries had been its endeavour to conciliate the United States and facilitate the securing of its help by pretending to agree with the aims of the United States policy when we knew those aims to be out of date and impossible of fulfilment. The only way to avoid further misunderstanding and embitterment for all concerned, he said, 6849-11
was to speak frankly and to point out that, while grateful for such help as the United States may in her own interest care to give toward recovery, it must be free from all conditions which make that recovery impossible. On that issue there is today no room for further pretence or equivocation. Mr. Amery said:
Our self-respect, as well as our sheer necessity, demands a clear and unmistakable declaration of British independence.
These trade agreements should, in my opinion, be defeated.
The failure of the government at Ottawa to grapple with the urgent problems facing it, its "wait and see" policy, is responsible for the conditions in which we find ourselves today. Its "wait and see" policy has brought on this dollar crisis. Ottawa has failed to put recovery before party legislation. We have had nothing but party legislation from the Minister of Agriculture, (Mr. Gardiner). Ottawa has completely failed in the last two years to put Canada's recovery before party legislation. Canada supported the loan to Britain and the Bretton Woods agreement but failed to put first things first. It should put its own house in order and have a new deal and a new wage policy such as I have enunciated.
These agreements would upset our whole economic policy, the policy which we have followed since confederation. They mean out-and-out free trade. They sound the death knell of preferential trade within the empire. Our primary duty is to secure redress of the grievances of our people. The government at Ottawa has shown no evidence of vision, and "without vision the people perish".
The totalitarian state over-run by internationalism is a menace and socialism, of the Marx and Lenin type now copied in Britian, has a real threat to the freedom and liberty of the individual. I am absolutely opposed to dictatorship over the people of Canada by Ottawa and the handing out to a vaster bureaucracy than has ever been attempted here the control over lives and property of individuals proposed by the present government. I clearly saw in December. 1945, the coming of this tragedy when I opposed strongly the Bretton Woods and American loan agreement which has been the cause and effect of this dollar situation and, along with the United States loan, has led to attempts to liquidate and dissolve the British empire.
I would use the old national policy of protection for capital and labour and make both of them conform to humanizing industry in Canada and not nationalizing it. I would
Tariffs and Trade

harmonize industry, not nationalize it. I stand where I have always stood, for a national policy brought up to date to meet after-the-war conditions and for the mother country. I have never abandoned and never will abandon such a position reached by me over the years from intensive study and deep conviction. I am for liberty and freedom for industry. I am for eliminating its being hamstrung and being placed in a strait-jacket. I would humanize it and create a spirit of good will, with harmony, companionship and comradeship individually, providing a means and incentive to all workers and toilers to rise to the top by their own free will and by theit own ability, with a fair chance of equality of opportunity so as to acquire increased production and a higher standard of living. That is what is being done by such industries as the Bell Telephone Company and others, which are now doing so well. They are seeing to it that their employees take stock in these companies.
I do not know that I have anything further to say, except that we are at the parting of the ways, as I said in the house on the budget speech last June. I criticized the budget because it forgot all about the British empire. The policy that they should follow is the empire first, last and all the time. Trade should follow the flag and the flag the trade. I voted against the Bretton Woods agreement because I saw the dangers of liquidating empire trade and preferences. I said that the whole future of the mother country depended on the dominions. Without them she would become a second Denmark at the edge of Europe and we would have little or nothing to say in the peace. The resources of the empire are vastly superior to those of Russia and the United States because they are land entity propositions, while the empire is spread over the seven seas. At no time has it been more necessary for Canada to give support, even if it is only moral support, to the motherland. Our foreign policy should be wrapped up with that of the mother country.
Britain has forty-seven million people. She can feed only some twenty-seven million of them. Where is she to find the food for the others without the help of the dominions? Mr. Churchill said the other day that twelve million people would have to migrate from the United Kingdom unless the policies in that country were changed because she is unable to support them.
Here we are sitting for weeks and months doing nothing. We sat here from last January until the 17th of July and the government of the day told us nothing about the Geneva agreements. We heard not one word about them, although the meetings were going on all 
the time. On February 5 the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) told us something about them. Canada refused Britain's bid to join Australia and New Zealand in empire conference before the Geneva trade talks, and these new Ottawa deals have upset the whole tariff policy of Canada since confederation.
As a matter of fact the present government never believed in the British empire in the first place. Many of them were free traders. Some hon. members to my left are free traders. They believe that the grain growing industry is north and south. Our best customer is Britain. She stood by us during the two wars.
I am glad to see the hon. member foi Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) in his seat tonight. I was down in his constituency in which Sir John A. Macdonald had a summer home. Sir John A. Macdonald visited Riviere du Loup for seventeen summers, from 1873 to 1890. I wanted to find out what was going on in Ottawa. I was told, "If I want to know what has been going on in Ottawa for the last eight months do not hang around Ottawa; do not hang around Montreal or Toronto or Quebec." That is why I went to Riviere du Loup and learned a lot. I asked one gentleman what he thought of Sir John A. Macdonald. He said to me with much respect that he was loved by the clergy and by the people. He said to me. "I do not know what you call it, but he had sixty-five seats in Quebec."
I do not object to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I have a great respect for him; I have known him for a long time. In fact his father used to sit on the bench with me when I was the manager of the Osgoode Hall football team, but that has nothing to do with the question before the house. I would not object to any prime minister, be he Liberal, Conservative or anything else, during the war when the enemy was at our gates, announcing policies himself, and all that kind of thing. But the war is over. What should a political party do? A political party should stick to its principles. Hon. gentlemen opposite have forgotten all about their principles. They abandoned the British preferences in 1938 and others followed them. The present Minister of Agriculture was a free trader. He did not believe in protection. What has he done since the war? They have had fifteen or sixteen different forms of protection. If you have 400 acres and you sowed only 100 acres the government would give you a war bonus of some kind, a bonus not to grow a crop at all.

Tariffs and Trade
As I say, if a party sticks to its principles it need have nothing to fear, but when it runs away from its principles that is another matter. People sometimes forget why political parties were formed. They were formed to protect the greatness of the country and the welfare of its people. When one criticizes the party system he forgets its great virtues; he forgets what the mother country gave to the dominions and what she has done for the people of the world.
The central provinces of Quebec and Ontario are great industrial provinces. These provinces should be consulted before this house is divided. I did not like the idea of Bretton Woods and I oppose it. I believe this measure should go to a committee of the House of Commons, and if we have not time to deal with it before Christmas, then we should take a recess. We should not give up the British preference.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) for his reference to his trip to my constituency. Everybody was delighted to meet him. We had heard about him as the great and perennial member for Toronto during the first war and several years thereafter, and we know he has done more for the city of Toronto than any other living man. Therefore, when he came to my constituency he was not a stranger. Everybody was delighted to meet him. I invite all my colleagues to come to my constituency. The Conservatives will have an opportunity to make a pilgrimage to the house where Sir John A. Macdonald spent so many summers, at St. Patrick; and the Liberals may visit Mr. Taschereau, a former premier of Quebec; so that everybody will find some reason to visit that finest part of the lower St. Lawrence district.
We are discussing now, Mr. Speaker, an item under the international trade organization which is not yet in force. We have the Geneva draft charter, but it is still a draft charter because the international trade organization is not yet in force, and it will be in force only when it is ratified at Havana and is approved by the various parliaments of the countries which sent representatives to Geneva. We are discussing the future of trade, naturally; and if this parliament adopts this agreement, we shall not gain much from it if it is not adopted by all the other countries.
At the opening of the house I took the first opportunity to say that I do not believe in multilateral agreements. I remember the time when Mr. Bennett was Prime Minister and when there was a world economic conference which took place somewhere in London. It was a complete failure. It was impossible for 5849-lli
the nations to come to an agreement regarding trade. It will not be surprising to me if the' same thing happens now. In my humble view these world conferences are just an opportunity for some people to travel all over the world and discuss various matters without any fruitful results. I mentioned that Russia was-trying to cut the grass under the feet of Uncle Sam. In the New York Times of May 5 of last year, one will see that Russia outbid the United States for Mexican sisal.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext: For Mexican what?

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mexican sisal. My hon. friend knows about it. He knows everything Also they were looking for henequen. The report states that Yucatan henequen purchasers seek modern machinery but found difficulties in the United States, and the Russians were ready to supply the machinery in order to have the contract. What was surprising was that they had gold to offer in payment. It was probably gold that was coming from the bank for international settlements. They were controlling the governments of some of the Balkan countries. That gave them some opportunity to get gold. Whether the gold came from the Ural district in Russia I do not know, but they were outbidding the United States in South America and they were offering gold there. In the New York Times of May 12, 1946, I see this headline, "Russia penetrates Argentine markets", and the article goes on to state as follows:
The Soviet trade mission that has been working quietly but effectively since its arrival in-Buenos Aires several weeks ago has offered such-attractive. prices for linseed oil and other products in which .Russia is interested, that other nations are finding the competition intense. The United States representative of the combined' allied food board, William Jasspon, has been-unable to consummate what is regarded as a reasonable agreement for purchases.
And so on. I cannot read it all. But it shows that there was a trend in- Russian trade to take advantage of t-heir gold- to outbid United States purchasers of primary commodities in Central and South America. Some time ago I also read in one of the Montreal papers a dispatch from Reuters or the Associated Press to the effect that Russia was desiring more trade. Gold is not the only thing that is used for trade. During the war there was another standard of exchange, namely, cigarettes. In some countries of Europe one could go much farther by using cigarettes as a means of exchange than by any other means. But now the position is entirely different. We have two standards of currency at the present time. There is gold and there is the United States dollar, and there is also wheat.
Tariffs and Trade

During the war I could never understand the reducing of wheat acreage, when it was so [DOT]easy to keep wheat and grain not only for ihuman consumption but for future exchange. At the present time Russia is bartering wheat or selling wheat to the western European [DOT]countries such as Belgium, the Netherlands *and France and is also selling wheat to Great Britain. To show that multilateral agreements *are not worth anything, according to published information which has appeared in the press, the government of Great Britain is trying to make bilateral agreements with Sweden and three other countries. If multilateral agreements were so good, do you think, sir, that Great Britain would not be satisfied with them but would go to the trouble of making bilateral agreements with Sweden and three other countries now, and probably the rest of the world afterwards, as has always been the case? How is it that we have to change the trade practices that have existed for such a long time? From the beginning of the world trade has been between two persons, two groups or two countries. Now everyone is [DOT]called together to reach an agreement and [DOT]we have a tower of babel and an agreement that can be a success only when all the interested parties have approved it and assumed some responsibilities in accordance with it.
At the present time some people find it strange that the Canadian Press does not pay much attention to what is going on at Havana. Since the beginning of the session, I have bought the New York Times; I am not a regular reader of that newspaper, though I appreciate it. I have gone through all the copies of the New York Times since last Friday, and the only reference I found there to the Havana conference was in the issue of Saturday, December 6. It was a special dispatch by Russell Porter from Havana, under the heading, "United nations body accepts Mexican project." That project was an amendment to article 70 of the draft charter, to create another committee.
You know, Mr. Speaker, in the first place the international trade organization consists of the conference to which all member nations belong. In addition, there is an executive board, a tariff committee, a staff commission and a technical commission. The Mexican delegate suggested, in addition, an economic development committee whose purpose it would be to improve communications and transportation facilities between various countries. In the two and a half hours debate, this amendment was supported by the delegates of Venezuela, Cuba, Greece, Turkey, India, Costa Rica. Egypt and China, and .opposed by Australia, Britain and Sweden. It
	,
was the divergence of views between economically developed countries and economically undeveloped countries which gave the Mexican delegate the idea for the formation of that new committee. The amendment obtained a majority of the votes in spite of the fact that it was opposed by Britain, Sweden and Australia. Apparently Canada did not vote on it. My point is that here was at least one of the best informed newspapers in America, the New York Times, with news from all over the world, giving such little space in its jumbo edition of Saturday; and even the news given there is not of very great importance.
I regret very much the acreage reduction which took place during the war. It is unfortunate that we did not have a reserve of wheat to trade with other countries, which would have put us on the same footing as Russia. Then we would have been able, not only to help other countries, but to give them help without imposing political considerations, as Russia has been doing for some time. If we had sent large quantities of our gold to the United States we would have had that reserve of wheat to trade with the whole world, and would have been able to impose Canadian conditions in regard to trade.
I can imagine what it was like at Geneva. There would be a large table, and sitting around it would be delegates from all over the world. How could they discuss the sale of their goods to other nations? God has established different climates throughout the world so that men could trade together. There is the cold climate, the temperate climate and the tropical climate. Each part of the world produces different commodities. Probably this was done in order to give mankind the opportunity to practise brotherhood. And of course transportation facilities are required to bring to each country the things it does not produce. But how can anything be done when the delegates are sitting together at these world conferences? Any progress made is not achieved at the sittings of the conference but through private talks between the delegates of the various nations. Therefore I imagine, if there are worthy trade representatives of some nations there, they take advantage of the conference to promote the trade of their own countries. They try to get in touch with the delegates of other countries to discuss privately the things that concern them. So what happens at the general meetings is just academic talk about the reduction of tariffs.
How can we speak about the reduction of tariffs when there is a wall preventing exchanges between neighbour countries such as Canada and the United States? Sometimes

Tariffs and Trade
it is necessary to put an embargo on the export of certain Canadian products when we do not have enough for our own consumption, but on the other hand we must do our best to trade with the other nations and facilitate that trade as much as possible. One reason we are insisting upon an embargo on grain, for instance, is that livestock is about to be destroyed because of the present shortage and high prices of coarse grains. How shall we be able to fulfil the obligations entered into by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) with the government of Great Britain and other governments if our farmers are not helped to raise their stock?
These matters are very difficult. There is a feeling held by some that we must have broad views on trade and that we must consider the future of other nations. I am for that, to a certain extent, provided that we look after our own people first and follow the old principle that charity begins at home.
Yesterday I heard my hon. friend the leader of the Social Credit group (Mr. Low) speaking about economic nationalism. He did not dare to use the word "patriotism." It is only patriotism to help the people of our own country. If we have to exteriorize our charitable feelings, then we must do so in the first place for those who are near us. Our country must be kept in good shape if we want to help others.
What is the use of giving all we have to other countries, when we deprive our own fellow citizens of what they are entitled to get from the soil of this country of ours? I may be called names because I express that view; but my deep feeling is that in the first place we must assist those who are citizens of this country. They must be as prosperous as they possibly can be in order to help others.
What is happening with those financial policies, extolled so highly in later years? We are destroying the purchasing power of the Canadian people. We are destroying private ownership. Not so many years ago in France the communist party was banned. France was a country which was against communism. How did it become communistic? It was precisely because the right of ownership was destroyed and the middle class lost its property. And, with the devaluation of the franc the French people said:	"We might as well
be communists, nothing is left to us."
I warned the government, during the war and after it, about foolish expenditures. I live in the country, and I know very well that when the tap on the first floor is left wide open the tap on the second floor does not flow very well. During and after the war everything was good if it was not done for Canada.
We had to do this; we had to do that:	we
had to finance the British empire. What do we know about our trade? Let me at this point read to the house a question I asked in 1943 of the then minister of Finance:
Mr. Pouliot:	We have totals of exports to
Great Britain, so many millions of dollars. Do these totals include exports in virtue of the gift legislation of last year, or of the lend-lease act.
Mr. Ilsley:	Our export figures would include
all that we exported, whether paid for out of the billion dollar gift or not. It would include those.
Afterwards, when I asked him if he could establish the difference between our exports which were paid to us and our exports which were paid from the credit that we were giving to another country, he said he could not tell us.
Trade figures are not real. What we called our trade was not real. It was paid from what was coming from the taxation of Canadian citizens. What happened with that? Taxes piled higher and higher, and those who voted for the loan-gifts had not the right to complain about increases in taxation because those gifts were the cause of the taxation. If we had strikes and difficulties among working men it was precisely because their salaries were cut at the source for the payment of taxes resulting from prodigality and excessive expenditures during the war. And, during the war those who protested against it were pointed out and described as bad Canadians, unworthy of our famous Canadian citizenship, and as disloyal British subjects.
We were ahead of our time. We were telling the house at that time what some lion, gentlemen arc telling it now. But they have-not the right to speak at this time, because-if we go back to those days we see what they did at that time and find that their record is not enviable. That is that.
What I regret is that those men who were placed in key positions by the Bennett administration at the time of the great depression and who, to a large extent, were responsible for that depression, have been maintained in office. When I denounced them I was always rebuked, and they were described as wizards. It is hard for a member of parliament to stand alone, or nearly alone, and to protest on behalf of his fellow citizens in order to protect them against the folly and stupidity of those who have been described as great geniuses.
Let us look at the Department of Finance; look at the Bank of Canada. There you see the men who hold the strings of power in this country. It is impossible to kick them out. I suggested at one time that we pay an
Tariffs and Trade

annuity of SI00,000 a year to one of them, to get rid of him. It was scandalous. But at the present time we have to stand by them.
During the war the economy of Canada was that of Schacht in Germany. Not only that, but the yearly reports of the Bank of Canada explained to us that the only possible economy of Canada during the war was tnat of Germany. Germany was only self-supporting. However, not only did we do that, but we supported the whole British empire; and it was not called the British empire, because in this country some people, not I, are afraid to call things by their right names. It was called the sterling area. We financed the whole sterling area. We had not enough backbone for that and now we are suffering for il.
Some people will say: "We have dominion ."status and are much better off." We are not only a dominion, but we are Canada just Canada now. How have some English writers described the status of various parts of the [DOT]empire? I quote here from a release of the British Information Services, which is an agency of the British government located at 30 Rockefeller Plaza, New York City, which states at page 6:
Thus "Dominion Status" is the most advanced stage of a process of political evolution or change -like the change from the frog's egg through the tadpole stage to the complete frog. ^ If we had some sixty frogs, tadpoles and frog's eggs of various age3 in a pond, they would change and grow"; the eggs becoming tadpoles; the tadpoles frogs; the frogs growing bigger and perhaps leaving the pond. At any moment, of course, .*some would already be changed into frogs; some -would still be in the egg. some in the early tad-[DOT]pole stage; and some nearly transformed, but -with a rudimentary and fast disappearing tail. :Some might be very slow to hatch out of the egg, and others might stay too long in the tadpole stage-but in the end they would all change and grow up. This is a parable of the British commonwealth and empire.
If hon. members are not satisfied I will quote what was said by a former secretary of state for the dominions-it used to be for the colonies-Malcolm MacDonald. When he spoke before the Royal Empire Society in London he said:
Some day Great Britain could conceivably lose Canada as a member of the empire, if she ever forces Canada to choose between the United States and Britain. If she wishes to avoid that loss, Britain had better recognize the toughness of Canadian-United States ties. Britain must "conduct her affairs so that Canada will never have to make the choice between .1 . the United Kingdom and . . . the United States."

Canada is under the influence of American thought and ideas, but she is still essentially British in instinct. Britain's job is to keep Canada that way.
They are here to create trouble. I am not speaking of the governor general for whom I have the highest regard, but I do say that the office of the high commissioner for Canada is just a nest of spies. One woman who worked there for fifteen years unmolested is now in jail. I am all for the people of England because they are thinking along the right lines. I could quote to the house many letters which women in England have written to me telling of their despair under the socialist government that they now have in Great Britain. Why should we be tolerant of the government of Great Britain when the British people themselves complain about it and when we read in the press that Winston Churchill has called the present government of Great Britain incompetent? I think he was unjust to Mr. Attlee because I believe he is a great man, but he is surrounded with many incompetent ministers. Everyone knows that, and no one knows it better than the English people. If hon. friends are doubtful about this I can show them letters , that I have read outside the house. I can show them letters which I have received recently, in which these people state that they expect a black Christmas because of the stupidity of some of the ministers and the measures they have put through.
In trade there is nothing so good as to mind you own business. I cannot praise the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) too highly for the trouble he has taken to visit other countries in order to promote Canadian trade. He was exceedingly well received in South America, but it was Canadian businessmen who paved the way for his trip there and to South Africa, and to countries in Europe. His trip would have been a complete success if he had not changed his mind when he arrived in England, for what reason I do not know.
It is possible to trade with England. It is possible to trade with the old merchants of London, Liverpool, Manchester and other places. How is it that with a socialist government it is impossible for Canadian people or any other people to trade with British people except through their stupid government? Because the British government is socialistic, are we bound to adopt socialistic measures in order to deal with them? Are we to deprive Canadian businessmen of their rights and initiative in connection with trade with Great Britain and other nations of the world? Merchants and traders must have the opportunity

Tariffs and Trade
of access to all markets of the world in complete freedom and the necessary transportation facilities must be provided.
Has the businessman of this country been paid the tribute he deserves? Was the government alone responsible for the magnificent war effort of Canada? What about the businessmen big and small, the middle class of the country, who suffered so many hardships and sacrifices during the war in order to give their staffs employment and to make a success of their business and of the war effort of Canada? Who else did that if it was not the Canadian merchant, the Canadian businessman, the Canadian importer and the Canadian exporter? That is why it is so dangerous to interfere with personal trade and that is why I am opposed to socialism which is the control of all human activities by the state.
There is no practical difference between socialism and communism. We have free enterprise when the businessmen of the country are not-fearful of the government, when they do not have to depend upon the government for the success of their business, when they can go on by themselves without the need of any crutches. There should be complete freedom so that every citizen can deal with whom he wants to deal, so that he can buy his products from whom he wants to buy. He may have to pay some duty which will go into the coffers of the state for public business, and that is all right, provided that the amount is not exaggerated.
You have socialism in a country when the businessmen, both large and small, are fearful of bureaucracy. You have socialism when a man cannot consider himself independent, when he cannot consider himself a free man. We cannot speak of free initiative in this country.	I remember the ramblings and
mistakes and blunders made by the same men who are in charge today. At the time of the Bennett government they were, considered geniuses. I can remember how the tariff board was composed of Tories who were not kicked out when the Liberal party came into power in 1935. They were there until the war came on, in order to draft Liberal tariff policy. It was impossible to kick them out; they were there forever. It was the same thing in the Bank of Canada, the Department of Finance and other departments. I am not censuring all the high officials of this country because some are very good. But others are dangerous and there should be a combing out and a clean-up.
I look at hon. gentlemen who complain about bureaucracy in the abstract, and I challenge them to denounce any one of the key men who are making the policies of this
country but who cannot draft a motion for the order paper. They know nothing. They are considered great because my hon. friends and the people of this country are too credulous and ready to accept everything that is said by them.
I think of the farmers of my country and of the merchants and businessmen. I want to see them prosperous and happy. There is no change in the present policy. It is no different from the policy of the time of Bennett. There was a world conference then, and we have a world conference now. It was called an economic conference then. Now it is the Geneva conference. Only the name is changed. It is the same policy. It is the same people who were there. They have no imagination. They are ready to ape everything they see anywhere else, and they are not helpful to the Canadian businessman. Every time we approach them they are like the Almighty, and the member of parliament is always wrong and the bureaucrat always right. It is impossible to make them change their minds. There is the procrastination of bureaucracy that we have here today. It is time to stop it, and unless those men are put out, the agreements that are before us now will be worth nothing.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as representing a constituency which has a- large proportion of men engaged in the fishing industry, either directly or indirectly, I should like to say a few words as to the effect which these trade treaties may have upon that industry.
But before doing so, I would crave permission to say a word of welcome to an old comrade in arms of mine, the new Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Gregg). He and I have shared the difficulties, hardships and anxieties of two world wars. I wish him well in the very difficult task that he now has taken on. I do not believe that there is any industry in Canada which needs a firm and guiding hand more than the fishing industry of our country because, even before these agreements were brought in, that fishing industry was in a precarious state owing to the drop in prices and the tremendous price increases there have been in all types of fishing gear.
I said, sir, that many of the people of my constituency are engaged in fishing. They are the fishermen who live in small villages and who go out in boats to catch the fish. They are those who are engaged in the canning industry, and they are those who service the boats of the industry.
Before the war, the great bulk of the canned salmon put up on the coast of British
Tariffs and Trade

Columbia was sent to the British market. I believe that somewhere in the neighbourhood of 400,000 cases of salmon annually went over to Great Britain. When the war came, that amount was increased. Great Britain was prepared to take 100 per cent of our pack, with the result that literally over 1,000,000 cases of salmon per annum wont to the British market, and we had very small quantities made available for our Canadian market. Prior to the war, I believe that our Canadian market was able to absorb somewhere in the neighbourhood of 600,000 cases. As the war went on and finally was won, the demand was perhaps not so great in Great Britain, while the demand in Canada increased and a certain small percentage of the canned salmon pack each year was saved for the Canadian market.
Now we come to the conditions which arose during this year, and in which, owing to various causes, one of them being a shortage of United States dollars available to Great Britain, Great Britain was not able to take as much of our pack as she had taken previously. She is taking none at the present time. She turned elsewhere for the canned salmon that she needed for her market. She went to our old competitors, the Russian and Japanese markets, and within the last year she has been buying Kamchatka salmon as put up by the Japanese for the Russians and sold to Great Britain.
This year Canadian packers were not permitted to sell salmon to the United States market. The export permit controls prevented that. But these were lifted in September so far as pink salmon is concerned, and in October for other types of canned salmon. The result of that has been that, since September of this year, the equivalent in raw salmon of 150,000 eases of canned salmon lias been sent to the United States market. I cite that as an instance of what may happen when these trade agreements are brought into effect. I repeat, this year the equivalent of 150,000 cases of canned salmon has been exported in the form of raw salmon, not canned, but salmon caught by Canadian fishermen, to be canned in the United States.
What is the situation with reference to this great industry of British Columbia in so far as these new trade agreements are concerned? I suggest that there is no division of the fishing industry which will feel so sharply the effects of the new agreements as the canning industry of British Columbia. That industry will, when these agreements come into force, have lost fifty per cent of its preference in the United

Kingdom market and a large percentage, I believe thirty per cent, of its preferences in the markets of Australia and New Zealand.
The customs tariff on canned salmon entering the United States, as the house has been told, by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) earlier today, is twenty-five per cent ad valorem, and the duty is bound at that figure. At the same time the tariff on fresh and frozen salmon entering the United States was reduced by fifty per cent. The result of all this is that our canning industry is doomed. There is consequently an extreme shortage in the pack of canned salmon available for our domestic market and for Canadian export markets. This year there were a million cases of canned salmon allowed for the domestic market. That has been a case of filling up the pipeline with an amount in excess of what is normally used in Canada. But if this flow of raw salmon is to be permitted to go to United States canneries I see that our own Canadian canneries and all those who are employed in that industry will be in the gravest possible danger of being forced out of employment and the trade going from Canada to the United States.
I wish to draw this matter to the attention of the Minister of Fisheries because I believe it is essential that measures be taken at once to remedy that situation which I foresee. I know that in the trade agreements there are protective or escape clauses. I hope that they will be studied and that it will be seen possible to find some solution. When these agreements are put into force I hope that we shall be able to retain something of our British market and that we shall be able to retain our domestic market and the personnel who depend on that industry for their livelihood in British Columbia will be kept employed.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext: Coming from the constituency of Shel-burne-Yarmouth-Clare, I wish to say that I am heartily in favour of this Geneva trade agreement, and so are all the people from the southwest corner of Nova Scotia. Being a fishing area, we have always depended for our livelihood on free trade. Without free trade, or the greatest, measure of free trade possible, we starve. We suffered from that in the early days after confederation; but this Geneva agreement has given us the brightest outlook that we have seen since confederation. When I was a youngster I was brought up to look upon the days of 1911, when the Liberal government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier was defeated, as black days for my section of the country and for the maritime provinces in general.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
What is going on there now?

Tariffs and Trade

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I want to say that, as far as the fishing industry is concerned, we shall benefit from the United States concessions upon nearly all species and preparations of fish. Certain branches of the industry, which this spring were faced with a sharp drop in demand, will now have greater access to the United States market. The duty on fresh or frozen salmon and halibut has been cut from one cent to a half-cent a pound. The rates on fresh mackerel, formerly one cent a pound, and on frozen mackerel, formerly li cents, have both been reduced to three-quarters of a cent a pound. On fresh or frozen fillets of cod, haddock, hake, pollock, cusk and rose fish, within a quota, the tariff has been bound at li cents a pound. That is important news to the people of my constituency and they will welcome this trade agreement.
I think we all realize that, in these days of complex trade, multilateral agreements are necessary. Bilateral agreements are no longer sufficient in themselves. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said, we must be interested, not only in our customers, but also in our customers' customers. That is the only way whereby we can establish a freer form of world trade which will bring eventual prosperity, not only to Canada, but to the nations with which Canada is dealing and hopes to deal.
There is no doubt about it, if we want to bring about world peace and happiness we must bring about world prosperity. This Geneva trade agreement is the greatest step in that direction that I have ever seen or heard about. If we do not bring about healthy trade conditions among the nations of the world, eventually we shall probably drift back into hostilities. We have seen that before and might see it again, and this is our one great chance. I believe, sir, that this is no time for us to be playing politics. I am definitely not playing politics; I am in dead earnest.
